entries.literal: When Emperor Wu ascended the throne, Zhuang was gradually promoted to serve as Commandant of Lu, Governor of Jinan, and Chancellor of Jiangdu, rising to the Nine Ministers as Right Prefect of the Capital.

entries.zh: 以武安侯魏其時議，貶秩為詹事，遷為大農令。
entries.en: In the fallout from the dispute between the Marquis of Wu'an and the Marquis of Weiqi, he was demoted to Superintendent of the Imperial Household, and later transferred to the post of Grand Director of Agriculture.
entries.literal: Because of the dispute between the Marquis of Wu'an and the Marquis of Weiqi, he was demoted in rank to Superintendent of the Imperial Household, and then transferred to serve as Grand Director of Agriculture.

entries.zh: 當是時，太后弟武安侯蚡為丞相，中二千石來拜謁，蚡不為禮。
entries.en: At that time, Tian Fen, the Marquis of Wu'an and younger brother of the Empress Dowager, held the post of Chancellor. When officials of the two-thousand-bushel rank came to pay their respects, he would not deign to return their courtesies.
entries.literal: At that time, the Empress Dowager's younger brother, the Marquis of Wu'an, Tian Fen, was Chancellor. When officials of the two-thousand-bushel rank came to pay their respects, Fen did not return their courtesies.

entries.zh: 然黯見蚡未嘗拜，常揖之。
entries.en: Yet when Ji An encountered Tian Fen, he never once performed a full bow, offering only a casual salute with cupped hands.
entries.literal: Yet when An met Fen, he never once bowed, but merely gave a cupped-hands salute.

entries.zh: 天子方招文學儒者，上曰吾欲云云，黯對曰：「陛下內多欲而外施仁義，柰何欲效唐虞之治乎！」
entries.en: The Emperor was at that time actively courting men of letters and Confucian scholars. When the Emperor spoke of his grand ambitions, Ji An replied: 'Your Majesty harbors boundless desires within, yet makes an outward show of benevolence and righteousness—how can you hope to emulate the governance of Yao and Shun!'
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven was then recruiting men of letters and Confucian scholars. The Emperor said, "I wish to do such and such," and An replied: 'Your Majesty is inwardly full of desires yet outwardly makes a show of benevolence and righteousness—how can you hope to emulate the governance of Yao and Shun!'

entries.zh: 上默然，怒，變色而罷朝。
entries.en: The Emperor fell silent, his face darkening with rage, and abruptly dismissed the court.
entries.literal: The Emperor was silent, then grew angry, changed expression, and dismissed the court.

entries.zh: 公卿皆為黯懼。
entries.en: Every minister and grandee at court trembled for Ji An's sake.
entries.literal: The ministers and grandees were all afraid on An's behalf.

entries.zh: 上退，謂左右曰：「甚矣，汲黯之戇也！」
entries.en: After withdrawing, the Emperor said to his attendants: 'How blunt Ji An is!'
entries.literal: The Emperor withdrew and said to his attendants: 'How blunt Ji An is!'

entries.zh: 群臣或數黯，黯曰：「天子置公卿輔弼之臣，寧令從諛承意，陷主於不義乎？
entries.en: When some other ministers rebuked him, Ji An replied: 'The Son of Heaven appoints his ministers to advise and assist him—surely not to have them merely flatter and fawn, leading the sovereign into unrighteousness?
entries.literal: Some of the ministers reproached An, and An said: 'The Son of Heaven appoints ministers and grandees to assist and counsel him—would you have them merely flatter and comply, leading the ruler into unrighteousness?

entries.zh: 且已在其位，縱愛身，柰辱朝廷何！」
entries.en: Once a man holds such a position, even if he values his own skin, how can he bear to bring disgrace upon the court!'
entries.literal: Moreover, already holding such a position, even if one cherishes one's own life, what of the disgrace to the court!'

entries.zh: 黯多病，病且滿三月，上常賜告者數，終不愈。
entries.en: Ji An was plagued by illness, and on one occasion was bedridden for nearly three months. The Emperor repeatedly granted him sick leave, yet he never fully recovered.
entries.literal: An was often ill, and his illness lasted nearly three months. The Emperor frequently granted him leave, but he never recovered.

entries.zh: 最後病，莊助為請告。
entries.en: When he fell ill for the last time, Zhuang Zhu petitioned the Emperor on his behalf for an extension of leave.
entries.literal: The last time he fell ill, Zhuang Zhu petitioned for leave on his behalf.

entries.zh: 上曰：「汲黯何如人哉？」
entries.en: The Emperor asked: 'What sort of man is this Ji An, after all?'
entries.literal: The Emperor said: 'What kind of man is Ji An?'

entries.zh: 助曰：「使黯任職居官，無以踰人。
entries.en: Zhuang Zhu replied: 'If Ji An were judged solely on his ability to handle official duties, he would be no better than any other man.
entries.literal: Zhuang Zhu said: 'If An were judged merely by performing his official duties, he would not surpass other men.

entries.zh: 然至其輔少主，守城深堅，招之不來，麾之不去，雖自謂賁育亦不能奪之矣。」
entries.en: But when it comes to safeguarding a young sovereign, he would hold the fortress with unyielding resolve—no summons could lure him away, and no command could dislodge him. Even men who fancy themselves the equals of Meng Ben and Xia Yu could not wrest his loyalty from him.'
entries.literal: But when it comes to guarding a young ruler, he would hold the fortress deep and firm—beckoned, he would not come; waved away, he would not leave. Even those who consider themselves as brave as Ben and Yu could not take it from him.'

entries.zh: 上曰：「然。
entries.en: The Emperor said: 'Just so.
entries.literal: The Emperor said: 'Indeed.

entries.zh: 古有社稷之臣，至如黯，近之矣。」
entries.en: The ancients spoke of ministers devoted to the altars of state—Ji An comes close to that ideal.'
entries.literal: In ancient times there were ministers of the altars of soil and grain; as for An, he comes close to that.'

entries.zh: 始黯列為九卿，而公孫弘、張湯為小吏。
entries.en: When Ji An first took his place among the Nine Ministers, Gongsun Hong and Zhang Tang were still petty officials.
entries.literal: At first, An was ranked among the Nine Ministers, while Gongsun Hong and Zhang Tang were still minor officials.

entries.zh: 及弘、湯稍益貴，與黯同位，黯又非毀弘、湯等。
entries.en: As Gongsun Hong and Zhang Tang gradually rose to stand at his level, Ji An continued to denounce them.
entries.literal: When Hong and Tang gradually rose in rank and stood at the same level as An, An once again criticized and reviled Hong, Tang, and their ilk.

entries.zh: 已而弘至丞相，封為侯；
entries.en: In time, Gongsun Hong ascended to the Chancellorship and was enfeoffed as a marquis;
entries.literal: Before long, Hong rose to Chancellor and was enfeoffed as a marquis;

entries.zh: 湯至御史大夫；
entries.en: Zhang Tang rose to the office of Imperial Secretary;
entries.literal: Tang rose to Imperial Secretary;

entries.zh: 故黯時丞相史皆與黯同列，或尊用過之。
entries.en: and men who had once served as clerks under the Chancellor now held the same rank as Ji An—or had even surpassed him.
entries.literal: thus the clerks of the Chancellor's office in An's time all held the same rank as An, or were honored and employed above him.

entries.zh: 黯褊心，不能無少望，見上，前言曰：「陛下用群臣如積薪耳，后來者居上。」
entries.en: Ji An, being a man of narrow patience, could not conceal his resentment. In an audience with the Emperor, he stepped forward and declared: 'Your Majesty employs his ministers the way one stacks firewood—the latest additions always end up on top.'
entries.literal: An, being narrow-hearted, could not help feeling some resentment. When he saw the Emperor, he came forward and said: 'Your Majesty uses his ministers like stacking firewood—the latecomers are placed on top.'

entries.zh: 上默然。
entries.en: The Emperor said nothing.
entries.literal: The Emperor was silent.

entries.zh: 有閒黯罷，上曰：「人果不可以無學，觀黯之言也日益甚。」
entries.en: After Ji An had withdrawn, the Emperor remarked: 'A man truly cannot afford to neglect his studies. Just look at how Ji An's remarks grow more outrageous by the day.'
entries.literal: After a while, when An had withdrawn, the Emperor said: 'A man truly cannot do without learning. Observe how An's words grow more excessive by the day.'

entries.zh: 居無何，匈奴渾邪王率眾來降，漢發車二萬乘。
entries.en: Not long afterward, the Xiongnu King of Hunye led his people in surrender to the Han, and the court mobilized twenty thousand chariots to receive them.
entries.literal: Not long after, the Xiongnu Hunye King led his people to surrender, and the Han mobilized twenty thousand chariots.

entries.zh: 縣官無錢，從民貰馬。
entries.en: The government treasury was empty, so horses had to be requisitioned on credit from the common people.
entries.literal: The government had no funds and borrowed horses from the people on credit.

entries.zh: 民或匿馬，馬不具。
entries.en: Some people hid their horses, and the required number could not be assembled.
entries.literal: Some of the people hid their horses, and the full number of horses could not be gathered.

entries.zh: 上怒，欲斬長安令。
entries.en: The Emperor was furious and wanted to have the Magistrate of Chang'an beheaded.
entries.literal: The Emperor was angry and wished to execute the Magistrate of Chang'an.

entries.zh: 黯曰：「長安令無罪，獨斬黯，民乃肯出馬。
entries.en: Ji An said: 'The Magistrate of Chang'an bears no guilt. If you must behead someone, behead me, and the people will willingly bring out their horses.
entries.literal: An said: 'The Magistrate of Chang'an is without guilt. Behead me alone, and the people will be willing to bring out their horses.

entries.zh: 且匈奴畔其主而降漢，漢徐以縣次傳之，何至令天下騷動，罷獘中國而以事夷狄之人乎！」
entries.en: Moreover, these Xiongnu have abandoned their own lord to surrender to us. We need only pass them along from district to district at a leisurely pace—why must we throw the entire empire into turmoil, exhausting the resources of China to pamper barbarian peoples!'
entries.literal: Moreover, the Xiongnu have betrayed their lord and surrendered to the Han. The Han should slowly relay them along from county to county—why must it cause such upheaval throughout the empire, exhausting China to serve barbarian people!'

entries.zh: 上默然。
entries.en: The Emperor made no reply.
entries.literal: The Emperor was silent.

entries.zh: 及渾邪至，賈人與市者，坐當死者五百餘人。
entries.en: When the Hunye people arrived, more than five hundred merchants who had traded with them were convicted and sentenced to death.
entries.literal: When the Hunye people arrived, merchants who had traded with them were convicted and sentenced to death—over five hundred people.

entries.zh: 黯請閒，見高門，曰：「夫匈奴攻當路塞，絕和親，中國興兵誅之，死傷者不可勝計，而費以巨萬百數。
entries.en: Ji An requested a private audience at the High Gate and said: 'When the Xiongnu attacked our frontier passes and severed the marriage alliance, China raised armies to punish them. The dead and wounded were beyond counting, and the costs ran to hundreds of millions.
entries.literal: An requested a private audience and appeared at the High Gate, saying: 'When the Xiongnu attacked our frontier passes and broke off the marriage alliance, China raised armies to punish them. The dead and wounded were beyond counting, and the expenses ran to hundreds of millions.

entries.zh: 臣愚以為陛下得胡人，皆以為奴婢以賜從軍死事者家；
entries.en: In my humble view, Your Majesty should have given all captured Hu people as slaves to the families of soldiers who perished in the campaigns;
entries.literal: In my humble opinion, Your Majesty should take all the captured Hu people and make them slaves to be given to the families of soldiers who died in service;

entries.zh: 所鹵獲，因予之，以謝天下之苦，塞百姓之心。
entries.en: and would distribute the spoils among them, to repay the empire for its suffering and ease the resentment of the common people.
entries.literal: and distribute all the plunder to them, in order to repay the empire's suffering and satisfy the hearts of the common people.

entries.zh: 今縱不能，渾邪率數萬之眾來降，虛府庫賞賜，發良民侍養，譬若奉驕子。
entries.en: Even if that is no longer possible, now that the King of Hunye has led tens of thousands in surrender, you drain the treasury to shower them with rewards and mobilize honest citizens to wait upon and feed them—as though indulging a spoiled child.
entries.literal: Even if that is now impossible, when Hunye leads tens of thousands of his people to surrender, you empty the treasuries to reward them and mobilize law-abiding citizens to serve and provide for them, as though attending to a spoiled child.

entries.zh: 愚民安知市買長安中物而文吏繩以為闌出財物于邊關乎？
entries.en: How could simple commoners have known that trading goods in Chang'an would be construed by the legal clerks as smuggling across the frontier?
entries.literal: How would ignorant commoners know that buying and selling goods in Chang'an would be treated by the legal clerks as smuggling goods across the border passes?

entries.zh: 陛下縱不能得匈奴之資以謝天下，又以微文殺無知者五百餘人，是所謂『庇其葉而傷其枝』者也，臣竊為陛下不取也。」
entries.en: Your Majesty not only fails to use the wealth of the Xiongnu to repay the empire for its sufferings, but now would use petty legal technicalities to execute more than five hundred innocent people. This is the very meaning of the saying, "protecting the leaves while breaking the branches." I humbly advise Your Majesty against this course.'
entries.literal: Your Majesty has not only failed to use Xiongnu wealth to repay the empire, but would also use petty legal technicalities to execute over five hundred innocent people. This is what is called "sheltering the leaves while harming the branches." I humbly believe this is a course Your Majesty should not take.'

entries.zh: 上默然，不許，曰：「吾久不聞汲黯之言，今又復妄發矣。」
entries.en: The Emperor said nothing and refused the request, remarking: 'It has been a long time since I last heard from Ji An, and now he is spouting nonsense once again.'
entries.literal: The Emperor was silent and did not grant his request, saying: 'I have not heard Ji An's words for a long time, and now he speaks rashly again.'

entries.zh: 後數月，黯坐小法，會赦免官。
entries.en: Several months later, Ji An was found guilty of a minor infraction. Though an amnesty spared him punishment, he was dismissed from office.
entries.literal: Several months later, An was convicted of a minor offense, but happened to be pardoned by an amnesty and was dismissed from office.

entries.zh: 於是黯隱於田園。
entries.en: And so Ji An withdrew into retirement on his country estate.
entries.literal: Thereupon An retired to his fields and gardens.

entries.zh: 居數年，會更五銖錢，民多盜鑄錢，楚地尤甚。
entries.en: Some years later, the currency was reformed with the introduction of the five-zhu coin. Counterfeiting became rampant, particularly in the Chu region.
entries.literal: After several years, the currency was changed to the five-zhu coin. Many people counterfeited coins, and the problem was especially severe in the Chu region.

entries.zh: 上以為淮陽，楚地之郊，乃召拜黯為淮陽太守。
entries.en: The Emperor, recognizing that Huaiyang bordered the troubled Chu region, summoned Ji An from retirement and appointed him Governor of Huaiyang.
entries.literal: The Emperor considered that Huaiyang lay on the outskirts of the Chu region, and so summoned and appointed An as Governor of Huaiyang.

entries.zh: 黯伏謝不受印，詔數彊予，然後奉詔。
entries.en: Ji An prostrated himself and repeatedly declined to accept the seal of office. Only after repeated imperial insistence did he finally submit to the appointment.
entries.literal: An prostrated himself and declined to accept the seal. The Emperor repeatedly insisted, and only then did An accept the edict.

entries.zh: 詔召見黯，黯為上泣曰：「臣自以為填溝壑，不復見陛下，不意陛下復收用之。
entries.en: When summoned to a final audience, Ji An wept before the Emperor and said: 'I had resigned myself to dying in some ditch, never to see Your Majesty again. I never imagined you would call upon me once more.
entries.literal: When summoned by edict to an audience, An wept before the Emperor and said: 'Your servant believed he would die in some ditch and never again see Your Majesty. I did not expect Your Majesty would once more take me into service.

entries.zh: 臣常有狗馬病，力不能任郡事，臣願為中郎，出入禁闥，補過拾遺，臣之願也。」
entries.en: I am plagued by constant illness and lack the strength to administer an entire commandery. My wish is to serve as a Palace Gentleman, passing through the gates of the inner court, where I might help correct mistakes and fill in what has been overlooked—that is all I ask.'
entries.literal: Your servant is constantly afflicted by illness unworthy of mention, and lacks the strength to manage the affairs of a commandery. I wish to serve as a Palace Gentleman, going in and out of the forbidden gates, correcting faults and gathering what has been overlooked—this is your servant's wish.'

entries.zh: 上曰：「君薄淮陽邪？
entries.en: The Emperor replied: 'Do you think the post of Huaiyang beneath you?
entries.literal: The Emperor said: 'Do you look down on Huaiyang?

entries.zh: 吾今召君矣。
entries.en: I have called upon you for a reason.
entries.literal: I have now summoned you.

entries.zh: 顧淮陽吏民不相得，吾徒得君之重，臥而治之。」
entries.en: The officials and people of Huaiyang are at odds with one another. I rely on the weight of your authority alone—govern them, even if you must do so from your sickbed.'
entries.literal: It is just that the officials and people of Huaiyang are not getting along, and I rely solely on your authority—govern it even from your sickbed.'

entries.zh: 黯既辭行，過大行李息，曰：「黯棄居郡，不得與朝廷議也。
entries.en: After taking his leave, Ji An visited Li Xi, the Grand Herald, and said: 'I am being cast aside to a distant commandery, cut off from the deliberations of the court.
entries.literal: After An had taken his leave to depart, he visited Li Xi, the Grand Herald, and said: 'I, An, am being cast aside to a commandery and will no longer be able to participate in court deliberations.

entries.zh: 然御史大夫張湯智足以拒諫，詐足以飾非，務巧佞之語，辯數之辭，非肯正為天下言，專阿主意。
entries.en: But the Imperial Secretary Zhang Tang is clever enough to deflect any remonstrance and deceitful enough to disguise any wrong. He devotes himself to honeyed flattery and sophistic rhetoric, never willing to speak honestly for the good of the realm—he exists only to pander to the Emperor's whims.
entries.literal: Yet the Imperial Secretary Zhang Tang has enough cunning to deflect remonstrance and enough deceit to embellish his wrongs. He devotes himself to clever flattery and sophistic arguments, and is unwilling to speak forthrightly for the sake of the realm—he caters exclusively to the ruler's wishes.

entries.zh: 主意所不欲，因而毀之；
entries.en: Whatever the Emperor dislikes, Zhang Tang tears down;
entries.literal: Whatever the ruler dislikes, he accordingly vilifies;

entries.zh: 主意所欲，因而譽之。
entries.en: whatever the Emperor desires, he praises to the skies.
entries.literal: whatever the ruler desires, he accordingly praises.

entries.zh: 好興事，舞文法，內懷詐以御主心，外挾賊吏以為威重。
entries.en: He delights in stirring up trouble and twisting the law to his purposes. Behind closed doors he employs deceit to bend the Emperor's mind; in public he enlists corrupt officials to project an air of fearsome authority.
entries.literal: He delights in stirring up affairs, manipulating the letter of the law. Inwardly he harbors deceit to control the ruler's heart; outwardly he makes use of corrupt officials to bolster his own authority.

entries.zh: 公列九卿，不早言之，公與之俱受其僇矣。」
entries.en: You hold a seat among the Nine Ministers—if you do not speak out soon, you will share in his downfall.'
entries.literal: You hold a place among the Nine Ministers. If you do not speak out soon, you and he will both suffer punishment together.'

entries.zh: 息畏湯，終不敢言。
entries.en: But Li Xi was afraid of Zhang Tang and never dared to speak.
entries.literal: Li Xi feared Zhang Tang and in the end did not dare to speak.

entries.zh: 黯居郡如故治，淮陽政清。
entries.en: Ji An governed Huaiyang in his accustomed style, and the administration of the commandery became clear and well-ordered.
entries.literal: An governed the commandery in his accustomed manner, and the administration of Huaiyang was orderly and clean.

entries.zh: 後張湯果敗，上聞黯與息言，抵息罪。
entries.en: In time, Zhang Tang did indeed meet his downfall. When the Emperor learned of what Ji An had said to Li Xi, he punished Li Xi for his failure to speak up.
entries.literal: Later, Zhang Tang did indeed fall from power. The Emperor heard of the conversation between An and Li Xi, and punished Li Xi for his failure to act.

entries.zh: 令黯以諸侯相秩居淮陽。
entries.en: He ordered Ji An to continue at Huaiyang, now with the rank and salary of a Chancellor to a feudal lord.
entries.literal: He ordered An to remain in Huaiyang with the rank and salary of a Chancellor to a feudal lord.

entries.zh: 七歲而卒。
entries.en: Seven years later, he passed away.
entries.literal: After seven years, he died.

entries.zh: 鄭莊使視決河，自請治行五日。
entries.en: When Zheng Zhuang was sent on a mission to inspect a breach in the Yellow River, he requested five days to prepare for the journey.
entries.literal: When Zheng Zhuang was sent on a mission to inspect a breach in the Yellow River, he asked for five days to prepare for his journey.

entries.zh: 上曰：「吾聞『鄭莊行，千里不齎糧』，請治行者何也？」
entries.en: The Emperor said: 'I have heard it said that "when Zheng Zhuang travels, he needs no provisions for a thousand li." So why does he ask for time to prepare?'
entries.literal: The Emperor said: 'I have heard that "when Zheng Zhuang travels, he needs no provisions for a thousand li." Why does he ask for time to prepare his journey?'

entries.zh: 然鄭莊在朝，常趨和承意，不敢甚引當否。
entries.en: At court, however, Zheng Zhuang tended toward accommodation, deferring to the Emperor's wishes and never daring to press too firmly on questions of right and wrong.
entries.literal: However, at court Zheng Zhuang always sought to be agreeable and followed the Emperor's wishes, never daring to press strongly on matters of right and wrong.

entries.zh: 及晚節，漢征匈奴，招四夷，天下費多，財用益匱。
entries.en: In his later years, the Han was waging war against the Xiongnu and seeking to win over the barbarian peoples on all four frontiers. The expenses of the realm mounted, and the treasury grew ever more depleted.
entries.literal: In his later years, the Han was waging war against the Xiongnu and courting the four barbarian peoples. The expenses of the realm were great, and the treasury grew ever more depleted.

entries.zh: 莊任人賓客為大農僦人，多逋負。
entries.en: Zheng Zhuang had recommended his own associates and guests to serve as contractors for the Grand Director of Agriculture, and many of them absconded with their debts.
entries.literal: Zhuang recommended his personal guests and associates to serve as hired agents for the Grand Director of Agriculture, and many of them defaulted on their debts.

entries.zh: 司馬安為淮陽太守，發其事，莊以此陷罪，贖為庶人。
entries.en: When Sima An, then serving as Governor of Huaiyang, exposed the scandal, Zheng Zhuang was convicted and reduced to the status of a commoner, allowed to pay a fine in lieu of harsher punishment.
entries.literal: When Sima An, serving as Governor of Huaiyang, exposed the affair, Zhuang was convicted on account of it and redeemed himself as a commoner.

entries.zh: 頃之，守長史。
entries.en: Before long, he was reappointed to serve as Acting Chief Clerk.
entries.literal: Shortly after, he served as Acting Chief Clerk.

entries.zh: 上以為老，以莊為汝南太守。
entries.en: The Emperor, considering him too old for central office, appointed him Governor of Runan.
entries.literal: The Emperor considered him old and appointed Zhuang as Governor of Runan.

entries.zh: 數歲，以官卒。
entries.en: After several years, he died while still in office.
entries.literal: After several years, he died in office.

entries.zh: 黯為人性倨，少禮，面折，不能容人之過。
entries.en: By temperament, Ji An was proud and blunt, sparing little thought for social niceties. He would rebuke people to their faces and could not abide the failings of others.
entries.literal: An was by nature arrogant, lacking in courtesy, prone to rebuking people to their faces, and unable to tolerate the faults of others.

entries.zh: 合己者善待之，不合己者不能忍見，士亦以此不附焉。
entries.en: Those who shared his views he treated warmly, but those who disagreed he could hardly bear to look upon. For this reason, few officials chose to attach themselves to him.
entries.literal: Those who agreed with him he treated well, but those who disagreed he could not bear to see; officials likewise did not attach themselves to him because of this.

entries.zh: 然好學，游俠，任氣節，內行修絜，好直諫，數犯主之顏色，常慕傅柏、袁盎之為人也。
entries.en: And yet he was a man devoted to learning who kept company with wandering knights, a man who prized integrity and honor. His personal conduct was beyond reproach, and he delighted in speaking truth to power, frequently provoking the Emperor's displeasure. He had always admired the example set by Fu Bai and Yuan Ang.
entries.literal: Nevertheless, he loved learning, associated with knight-errants, upheld integrity and honor, maintained upright personal conduct, loved offering direct remonstrances, and frequently offended the ruler's countenance; he always admired the character of Fu Bai and Yuan Ang.

entries.zh: 善灌夫、鄭當時及宗正劉棄。
entries.en: He was close friends with Guan Fu, Zheng Dangshi, and Liu Qi, the Director of the Imperial Clan.
entries.literal: He was on good terms with Guan Fu, Zheng Dangshi, and the Director of the Imperial Clan, Liu Qi.

entries.zh: 亦以數直諫，不得久居位。
entries.en: Here too, his habit of blunt remonstrance prevented him from holding his position for long.
entries.literal: Also because of his frequent direct remonstrances, he could not remain long in his position.

entries.zh: 大將軍青侍中，上踞廁而視之。
entries.en: When the Grand General Wei Qing attended him at court, the Emperor would receive him while lounging casually by the latrine.
entries.literal: When the Grand General Wei Qing attended the Emperor at court, the Emperor would sit casually on the privy while receiving him.

entries.zh: 丞相弘燕見，上或時不冠。
entries.en: When Chancellor Gongsun Hong came for a private audience, the Emperor would sometimes receive him without even donning his formal cap.
entries.literal: When Chancellor Gongsun Hong came for informal audiences, the Emperor sometimes did not wear his cap.

entries.zh: 至如黯見，上不冠不見也。
entries.en: But when Ji An sought an audience, the Emperor would never receive him unless he was properly capped and dressed.
entries.literal: But when An came for an audience, the Emperor would not receive him without wearing his cap.

entries.zh: 上嘗坐武帳中，黯前奏事，上不冠，望見黯，避帳中，使人可其奏。
entries.en: Once, the Emperor was sitting informally in the military tent when Ji An approached to present a report. Caught without his cap, the Emperor spotted Ji An in the distance, retreated behind the curtains, and sent an attendant to approve the memorial on his behalf.
entries.literal: Once the Emperor was sitting in the military tent, and An came forward to report on affairs. The Emperor was not wearing his cap, and seeing An approaching from a distance, he withdrew behind the curtains and sent someone to approve his memorial.

entries.zh: 其見敬禮如此。
entries.en: Such was the degree of respect the Emperor accorded him.
entries.literal: Such was the respect and courtesy shown to him.

entries.zh: 張湯方以更定律令為廷尉，黯數質責湯於上前，曰：「公為正卿，上不能褒先帝之功業，下不能抑天下之邪心，安國富民，使囹圄空虛，二者無一焉。
entries.en: Zhang Tang had recently been appointed Commandant of Justice, tasked with revising the laws. Ji An repeatedly challenged him before the Emperor, declaring: 'You serve as Chief Justice, yet you have neither upheld the legacy of the former emperors above nor suppressed the wickedness in the hearts of the people below. You have failed to bring peace and prosperity to the nation, and the prisons remain full—you have accomplished neither of these goals.
entries.literal: Zhang Tang had just been made Commandant of Justice for revising the laws and statutes, and An repeatedly challenged and rebuked Tang before the Emperor, saying: 'You serve as the Chief Justice, yet above you cannot uphold the achievements of the former emperors, and below you cannot suppress the evil in the hearts of the people. You have neither brought peace and prosperity to the nation nor emptied the prisons—you have accomplished neither of these things.

entries.zh: 非苦就行，放析就功，何乃取斑皇帝約束紛更之為？
entries.en: Rather than striving to enforce proper conduct and build real achievements, why do you seize upon the late emperors' statutes only to throw them into confusion with endless revisions?
entries.literal: Rather than toiling to implement proper conduct and releasing what can be set aside to achieve merit, why instead do you take the late emperors' regulations and throw them into disorder with constant changes?

entries.zh: 公以此無種矣。」
entries.en: Mark my words—with such conduct, your line will come to an end.'
entries.literal: With this conduct, you will leave no descendants.'

entries.zh: 黯時與湯論議，湯辯常在文深小苛，黯伉厲守高不能屈，忿發罵曰：「天下謂刀筆吏不可以為公卿，果然。
entries.en: Whenever Ji An debated with Zhang Tang, Tang would invariably retreat into the fine print and petty technicalities of the law. Ji An, unbending and holding to his lofty principles, refused to yield, and at last erupted in fury: 'Everyone says that petty clerks should never be made ministers—and indeed it is true!
entries.literal: When An debated with Tang, Tang's arguments always relied on the fine points and petty technicalities of the law. An, unyielding and upholding lofty principles, could not be bent, and in fury burst out cursing: 'Everyone says that petty clerks of the knife and stylus should never be made ministers—how true that is!

entries.zh: 必湯也，令天下重足而立，側目而視矣！」
entries.en: It is Zhang Tang who has made the whole empire stand frozen in terror, barely daring to glance sideways!'
entries.literal: It is certainly Tang who has made the whole empire stand with their feet pressed together and look sideways in fear!'

entries.zh: 是時，漢方征匈奴，招懷四夷。
entries.en: At that time, the Han dynasty was waging campaigns against the Xiongnu and working to win over the barbarian peoples on all four frontiers.
entries.literal: At that time, the Han was engaged in campaigns against the Xiongnu and in attracting and pacifying the four barbarian peoples.

entries.zh: 黯務少事，乘上閒，常言與胡和親，無起兵。
entries.en: Ji An advocated simplicity in governance and, seizing every opportunity when the Emperor was at ease, would urge him to pursue peace through marriage alliances with the Hu rather than resorting to war.
entries.literal: An sought to keep affairs simple, and seizing upon the Emperor's leisure moments, he constantly advocated making peace through marriage alliances with the Hu rather than raising armies.

entries.zh: 上方向儒術，尊公孫弘。
entries.en: The Emperor, however, was increasingly drawn to Confucian scholarship and had elevated Gongsun Hong to a place of honor.
entries.literal: The Emperor was then turning toward Confucian learning and honoring Gongsun Hong.

entries.zh: 及事益多，吏民巧弄。
entries.en: As the affairs of state multiplied, officials and commoners alike grew ever more cunning and manipulative.
entries.literal: As affairs grew more numerous, officials and people became crafty and deceitful.

entries.zh: 上分別文法，湯等數奏決讞以幸。
entries.en: The Emperor took to parsing the fine points of the law with relish, and Zhang Tang and his ilk frequently submitted judicial verdicts to curry favor.
entries.literal: The Emperor discriminated finely among the provisions of the law, and Tang and others frequently submitted judicial decisions to gain favor.

entries.zh: 而黯常毀儒，面觸弘等徒懷詐飾智以阿人主取容，而刀筆吏專深文巧詆，陷人於罪，使不得反其真，以勝為功。
entries.en: Ji An was relentless in his criticism of the Confucians, confronting Gongsun Hong and others to their faces with the charge that they harbored nothing but deceit, dressing up their cleverness to flatter the Emperor. As for the legal clerks, he accused them of twisting the law and crafting specious accusations to entrap the innocent, denying them any chance of vindication—and counting each conviction as a triumph.
entries.literal: An constantly disparaged the Confucians, and confronted Gongsun Hong and his like to their faces, saying they merely harbored deceit and adorned their wisdom to flatter the ruler and win acceptance, while the clerks of the knife and stylus solely relied on harsh interpretations and clever slanders, entrapping people in guilt and preventing them from returning to truth, counting convictions as merit.

entries.zh: 上愈益貴弘、湯，弘、湯深心疾黯，唯天子亦不說也，欲誅之以事。
entries.en: Yet the Emperor continued to elevate Gongsun Hong and Zhang Tang, who in turn harbored a deep hatred of Ji An. The Emperor too had grown weary of Ji An and wished to find some pretext to put him to death.
entries.literal: The Emperor increasingly honored Hong and Tang, and Hong and Tang deeply hated An in their hearts. The Emperor too was displeased with An and wished to execute him on some pretext.

entries.zh: 弘為丞相，乃言上曰：「右內史界部中多貴人宗室，難治，非素重臣不能任，請徙黯為右內史。」
entries.en: When Gongsun Hong became Chancellor, he said to the Emperor: 'The district of the Right Prefect of the Capital is filled with nobles and members of the imperial clan—it is exceedingly difficult to govern. Only a minister of proven authority can manage it. I recommend that Ji An be transferred to the post of Right Prefect of the Capital.'
entries.literal: When Hong became Chancellor, he said to the Emperor: 'The jurisdiction of the Right Prefect of the Capital contains many nobles and members of the imperial clan and is difficult to govern. Unless a minister of established authority is appointed, the post cannot be filled. I request that An be transferred to serve as Right Prefect of the Capital.'

entries.zh: 為右內史數歲，官事不廢。
entries.en: Ji An served as Right Prefect of the Capital for several years, and the administration ran smoothly under his watch.
entries.literal: He served as Right Prefect of the Capital for several years, and official affairs were not neglected.

entries.zh: 大將軍青既益尊，姊為皇后，然黯與亢禮。
entries.en: Even after the Grand General Wei Qing had risen to ever greater eminence—his own sister having become Empress—Ji An continued to treat him as an equal.
entries.literal: After the Grand General Wei Qing had grown ever more honored, with his sister serving as Empress, An still treated him as an equal in courtesy.

entries.zh: 人或說黯曰：「自天子欲群臣下大將軍，大將軍尊重益貴，君不可以不拜。」
entries.en: Someone advised Ji An: 'The Son of Heaven expects every minister to defer to the Grand General, and his honor and rank only continue to grow. Surely you must bow before him.'
entries.literal: Someone advised An: 'Since the Son of Heaven wishes all the ministers to defer to the Grand General, and the Grand General is ever more honored and noble, you cannot fail to bow to him.'

entries.zh: 黯曰：「夫以大將軍有揖客，反不重邪？」
entries.en: Ji An replied: 'For the Grand General to have a guest who offers only a casual salute rather than a bow—does that not, in fact, add to his stature?'
entries.literal: An said: 'For the Grand General to have a guest who greets him with a cupped-hand salute rather than bowing—does that not rather add to his stature?'

entries.zh: 大將軍聞，愈賢黯，數請問國家朝廷所疑，遇黯過於平生。
entries.en: When the Grand General heard this, his admiration for Ji An only grew. He frequently sought Ji An's counsel on difficult matters of state, treating him with greater courtesy than he had shown in all their years of acquaintance.
entries.literal: When the Grand General heard this, he regarded An as even more worthy, and frequently sought his counsel on matters of doubt in the nation and the court, treating An with more respect than he had in all their years of acquaintance.

entries.zh: 天子既數征匈奴有功，黯之言益不用。
entries.en: As the Emperor's repeated campaigns against the Xiongnu bore fruit, Ji An's counsel was increasingly ignored.
entries.literal: Since the Son of Heaven had repeatedly campaigned against the Xiongnu with success, An's counsel was increasingly disregarded.

entries.zh: 卒後，上以黯故，官其弟汲仁至九卿，子汲偃至諸侯相。
entries.en: After his death, the Emperor, out of regard for Ji An, elevated his younger brother Ji Ren to the rank of the Nine Ministers and his son Ji Yan to the post of Chancellor to a feudal lord.
entries.literal: After his death, the Emperor, on account of An, appointed his younger brother Ji Ren to a position among the Nine Ministers and his son Ji Yan to the rank of Chancellor to a feudal lord.

entries.zh: 黯姑姊子司馬安亦少與黯為太子洗馬。
entries.en: Sima An, the son of Ji An's paternal aunt, had likewise served alongside him as an Attendant to the Crown Prince in their youth.
entries.literal: Sima An, the son of An's paternal aunt, had also served as Attendant to the Crown Prince alongside An in their youth.

entries.zh: 安文深巧善宦，官四至九卿，以河南太守卒。
entries.en: Sima An was a master of legal subtleties, clever, and adept at navigating the bureaucracy. He attained the rank of the Nine Ministers four separate times and eventually died while serving as Governor of Henan.
entries.literal: Sima An was learned in the fine points of the law, clever, and skilled at office-holding. He rose to the rank of the Nine Ministers four times and died as Governor of Henan.

entries.zh: 昆弟以安故，同時至二千石者十人。
entries.en: Thanks to Sima An's influence, ten of his brothers and cousins simultaneously held positions at the two-thousand-bushel rank.
entries.literal: Because of Sima An, his brothers and cousins at one time numbered ten who held the rank of two-thousand-bushel officials.

entries.zh: 濮陽段宏始事蓋侯信，信任宏，宏亦再至九卿。
entries.en: Duan Hong of Puyang began his career in the service of Xin, the Marquis of Gai, who placed great trust in him. Duan Hong twice rose to the rank of the Nine Ministers.
entries.literal: Duan Hong of Puyang initially served under the Marquis of Gai, Xin. Xin trusted Hong, and Hong also twice rose to the rank of the Nine Ministers.

entries.zh: 然衛人仕者皆嚴憚汲黯，出其下。
entries.en: And yet every official from Wei stood in awe of Ji An and acknowledged his superiority.
entries.literal: Yet all officials from Wei stood in awe of Ji An, and ranked below him.

entries.zh: 莊為太史，誡門下：「客至，無貴賤無留門者。」
entries.en: When Zheng Zhuang served as Grand Astrologer, he instructed his gatekeepers: 'When guests arrive, whether noble or humble, no one is to be kept waiting at the gate.'
entries.literal: When Zhuang served as Grand Astrologer, he instructed his doorkeepers: 'When guests arrive, whether noble or humble, none are to be kept waiting at the gate.'

entries.zh: 執賓主之禮，以其貴下人。
entries.en: He scrupulously observed the courtesies between host and guest, humbling himself before others despite his high rank.
entries.literal: He observed the proper courtesies between host and guest, using his own high position to humble himself before others.

entries.zh: 莊廉，又不治其產業，仰奉賜以給諸公。
entries.en: Zheng Zhuang was scrupulously honest and gave no thought to building up his personal fortune. He relied entirely on his official salary and imperial gifts to support his circle of associates.
entries.literal: Zhuang was incorruptible and did not tend to his own estates, relying on his salary and imperial gifts to provide for his various associates.

entries.zh: 然其餽遺人，不過算器食。
entries.en: Yet the gifts he gave were never more than simple utensils and plain food.
entries.literal: Yet the gifts he bestowed on others amounted to no more than simple utensils and food.

entries.zh: 每朝，候上之閒，說未嘗不言天下之長者。
entries.en: At every court session, whenever he found a moment with the Emperor, he never failed to put in a good word for the worthy men of the realm.
entries.literal: At each court session, when he found an opportune moment with the Emperor, his recommendations never failed to mention worthy men of the realm.

entries.zh: 其推轂士及官屬丞史，誠有味其言之也，常引以為賢於己。
entries.en: When he recommended scholars or his own subordinates and clerks, he spoke of them with such evident sincerity and relish that he invariably presented them as worthier than himself.
entries.literal: When recommending scholars and subordinate officials and clerks, he spoke of them with such genuine appreciation that he always made them seem worthier than himself.

entries.zh: 未嘗名吏，與官屬言，若恐傷之。
entries.en: He never addressed his officials by their personal names, and when speaking with subordinates, he seemed almost afraid of causing offense.
entries.literal: He never addressed his officials by their personal names, and when speaking with his subordinates, he acted as though afraid of offending them.

entries.zh: 聞人之善言，進之上，唯恐後。
entries.en: Whenever he learned of a good idea from someone, he would hasten to present it to the Emperor, as though afraid of being too late.
entries.literal: Whenever he heard a good proposal from someone, he would bring it before the Emperor, fearing only that he might be too late.

entries.zh: 山東士諸公以此翕然稱鄭莊。
entries.en: For all these reasons, the learned gentlemen east of the mountains spoke of Zheng Zhuang with unanimous admiration.
entries.literal: The scholars and gentlemen east of the mountains therefore united in praising Zheng Zhuang.

entries.zh: 鄭當時者，字莊，陳人也。
entries.en: Zheng Dangshi, whose courtesy name was Zhuang, was a native of Chen.
entries.literal: Zheng Dangshi, courtesy name Zhuang, was a man of Chen.

entries.zh: 其先鄭君嘗為項籍將；
entries.en: His forebear, Lord Zheng, had once served as a general under Xiang Yu;
entries.literal: His ancestor Lord Zheng had once served as a general under Xiang Ji;

entries.zh: 籍死，已而屬漢。
entries.en: After Xiang Yu's death, the family came under the allegiance of the Han.
entries.literal: After Xiang Ji died, the family subsequently submitted to the Han.

entries.zh: 高祖令諸故項籍臣名籍，鄭君獨不奉詔。
entries.en: When Emperor Gaozu ordered all former officers of Xiang Yu to register their names, Lord Zheng alone refused to comply.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor ordered all former ministers of Xiang Ji to register their names, Lord Zheng alone refused to obey the edict.

entries.zh: 詔盡拜名籍者為大夫，而逐鄭君。
entries.en: By imperial edict, all who had registered were appointed as Grandees, while Lord Zheng was driven into exile.
entries.literal: By edict, all who had registered were appointed as Grandees, while Lord Zheng was banished.

entries.zh: 鄭君死孝文時。
entries.en: Lord Zheng lived until the reign of Emperor Wen.
entries.literal: Lord Zheng died during the reign of Emperor Wen.

entries.zh: 及高皇帝誅項籍，舉兵圍魯，魯中諸儒尚講誦習禮樂，弦歌之音不絕，豈非聖人之遺化，好禮樂之國哉？
entries.en: When the High Emperor defeated Xiang Yu and his armies laid siege to Lu, the Confucian scholars within the city were still lecturing, reciting, and practicing the rites and music; the sounds of strings and song never ceased. Was this not the enduring legacy of the sage — a land truly devoted to ritual and music?
entries.literal: When the High Emperor destroyed Xiang Ji and raised troops to besiege Lu, the Confucian scholars within Lu were still lecturing, reciting, and practicing ritual and music, and the sounds of strings and singing did not cease — was this not the lingering influence of the sage, a land devoted to ritual and music?

entries.zh: 故孔子在陳曰：「歸與！
entries.en: And so Confucius, while in the state of Chen, once said: "Let me go home!
entries.literal: Therefore, Confucius, when he was in Chen, said: "Let me go home!

entries.zh: 歸與！
entries.en: Let me go home!
entries.literal: Let me go home!

entries.zh: 吾黨之小子狂簡，斐然成章，不知所以裁之。」
entries.en: The young men back home are ambitious yet unrestrained; they have produced splendid writings, but do not yet know how to shape them."
entries.literal: The young men of my school are impetuous and careless; they have produced brilliant patterns, but do not know how to trim them."

entries.zh: 夫齊魯之閒於文學，自古以來，其天性也。
entries.en: The devotion to literature and learning in the lands between Qi and Lu has been part of their very nature since ancient times.
entries.literal: As for the region between Qi and Lu and its devotion to literature and learning, from ancient times onward, this has been its innate character.

entries.zh: 故漢興，然後諸儒始得修其經藝，講習大射鄉飲之禮。
entries.en: Only after the founding of the Han were Confucian scholars at last able to resume their classical studies and practice the rites of the Great Archery Ceremony and the District Drinking Ceremony.
entries.literal: Therefore, when the Han arose, the Confucian scholars were at last able to cultivate their classical arts and lecture on and practice the rites of the Great Archery Ceremony and the District Drinking Ceremony.

entries.zh: 叔孫通作漢禮儀，因為太常，諸生弟子共定者，咸為選首，於是喟然嘆興於學。
entries.en: Shusun Tong devised the Han court rituals and was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies. The students and disciples who had helped establish these rites were all awarded top appointments, inspiring a great surge of admiration and enthusiasm for learning.
entries.literal: Shusun Tong created the Han court rituals and was thereupon made Grand Master of Ceremonies; the students and disciples who had helped establish them were all selected for the highest appointments, and at this they sighed with admiration and a passion for learning was aroused.

entries.zh: 然尚有干戈，平定四海，亦未暇遑庠序之事也。
entries.en: Yet with warfare still raging as the empire was being pacified, there was no time to attend to the affairs of the academies.
entries.literal: However, there were still weapons of war, and in pacifying the realm, there was no leisure for the affairs of schools.

entries.zh: 孝惠、呂后時，公卿皆武力有功之臣。
entries.en: In the reigns of Emperor Hui and Empress Dowager Lu, the high ministers were all men who had won their rank through military achievement.
entries.literal: During the time of Emperor Hui and Empress Dowager Lu, the high ministers were all men who had earned merit through military prowess.

entries.zh: 孝文時頗徵用，然孝文帝本好刑名之言。
entries.en: Under Emperor Wen, scholars were recruited to some extent, but the emperor himself was primarily drawn to the Legalist doctrines of punishment and terminology.
entries.literal: During the time of Emperor Wen, scholars were somewhat recruited and employed, but Emperor Wen was fundamentally fond of the doctrines of punishment and names.

entries.zh: 及至孝景，不任儒者，而竇太后又好黃老之術，故諸博士具官待問，未有進者。
entries.en: Under Emperor Jing, Confucian scholars found no favor, and Empress Dowager Dou was herself devoted to the teachings of Huang-Lao. The erudites merely held their posts and awaited inquiries, with none advancing in rank.
entries.literal: When it came to Emperor Jing, he did not employ Confucian scholars, and Empress Dowager Dou was furthermore fond of the arts of Huang-Lao; therefore the various erudites merely held office and awaited inquiries, with none being promoted.

entries.zh: 申公者，魯人也。
entries.en: Master Shen was a native of Lu.
entries.literal: Master Shen was a man of Lu.

entries.zh: 高祖過魯，申公以弟子從師入見高祖于魯南宮。
entries.en: When the High Ancestor passed through Lu, Master Shen accompanied his teacher as a student to have an audience with the High Ancestor at the Southern Palace of Lu.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor passed through Lu, Master Shen, as a disciple, accompanied his teacher to have an audience with the High Ancestor at the Southern Palace of Lu.

entries.zh: 呂太后時，申公游學長安，與劉郢同師。
entries.en: During the time of Empress Dowager Lu, Master Shen traveled to Chang'an to study and shared the same teacher as Liu Ying.
entries.literal: During the time of Empress Dowager Lu, Master Shen traveled to Chang'an to study, and he had the same teacher as Liu Ying.

entries.zh: 已而郢為楚王，令申公傅其太子戊。
entries.en: In time, Liu Ying became King of Chu and appointed Master Shen as tutor to his heir apparent, Wu.
entries.literal: Later, when Ying became King of Chu, he ordered Master Shen to tutor his heir apparent, Wu.

entries.zh: 戊不好學，疾申公。
entries.en: Wu had no love of learning and came to resent Master Shen.
entries.literal: Wu did not like learning and resented Master Shen.

entries.zh: 及王郢卒，戊立為楚王，胥靡申公。
entries.en: When King Ying died and Wu ascended as King of Chu, he sentenced Master Shen to servitude as a convict laborer.
entries.literal: When King Ying died and Wu was established as King of Chu, he had Master Shen punished as a convict laborer.

entries.zh: 申公恥之，歸魯，退居家教，終身不出門，復謝絕賓客，獨王命召之乃往。
entries.en: Humiliated, Master Shen returned to Lu and withdrew to teach from his home. For the rest of his life he never stepped outside his gate. He refused all visitors, and would venture forth only when summoned by royal command.
entries.literal: Master Shen was ashamed of this, returned to Lu, withdrew to teach at home, and for the rest of his life never went out. He further declined all guests and visitors, and would only go if summoned by the king's command.

entries.zh: 弟子自遠方至受業者百餘人。
entries.en: More than a hundred students came from distant places to study under him.
entries.literal: Disciples who came from distant places to receive his instruction numbered more than a hundred.

entries.zh: 申公獨以詩經為訓以教，無傳（疑），疑者則闕不傳。
entries.en: Master Shen taught solely through the explication of the Classic of Odes. He left no transmitted commentary, and where there was any doubt, he simply left a gap rather than pass on uncertain material.
entries.literal: Master Shen taught solely through the explication of the Classic of Odes; he had no transmitted commentary, and where there was doubt, he left gaps and did not transmit.

entries.zh: 董仲舒，廣川人也。
entries.en: Dong Zhongshu was a native of Guangchuan.
entries.literal: Dong Zhongshu was a man of Guangchuan.

entries.zh: 以治春秋，孝景時為博士。
entries.en: Through his mastery of the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was appointed an erudite during the reign of Emperor Jing.
entries.literal: Through his mastery of the Spring and Autumn Annals, he became an erudite during the reign of Emperor Jing.

entries.zh: 下帷講誦，弟子傳以久次相受業，或莫見其面，蓋三年董仲舒不觀於舍園，其精如此。
entries.en: He taught behind lowered curtains, and his disciples passed the teaching down by seniority, with each receiving instruction from the one before — some never even laid eyes on him. For three full years Dong Zhongshu never once glanced at his own garden. Such was the depth of his dedication.
entries.literal: He lowered his curtains and lectured; his disciples passed down the teaching by seniority, receiving instruction from one another, and some never even saw his face. For three years Dong Zhongshu never once looked out at his garden — such was his devotion.

entries.zh: 進退容止，非禮不行，學士皆師尊之。
entries.en: In every gesture and movement, he would do nothing that did not accord with ritual propriety. The scholars all revered him as a master.
entries.literal: In his every movement and manner, he would not act unless it accorded with ritual propriety, and all the scholars revered him as their master.

entries.zh: 今上即位，為江都相。
entries.en: When the present emperor ascended the throne, Dong Zhongshu was appointed Chancellor of Jiangdu.
entries.literal: When the present emperor ascended the throne, he was appointed Chancellor of Jiangdu.

entries.zh: 以春秋災異之變推陰陽所以錯行，故求雨閉諸陽，縱諸陰，其止雨反是。
entries.en: Drawing on the portents and anomalies recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he deduced the principles governing the interaction of yin and yang. To bring rain, he would suppress the yang forces and unleash the yin; to stop rain, he would do the reverse.
entries.literal: Using the portentous anomalies recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he deduced the principles by which yin and yang alternately operated; therefore, to seek rain he would shut off all the yang forces and release the yin forces, and to stop rain he would do the reverse.

entries.zh: 行之一國，未嘗不得所欲。
entries.en: Whenever he applied these methods within his domain, he never failed to get the result he sought.
entries.literal: When he practiced this within a single state, he never failed to obtain the desired result.

entries.zh: 中廢為中大夫，居舍，著災異之記。
entries.en: Midway through his tenure as chancellor, he was dismissed and given the lesser post of Palace Grandee. Living at his quarters, he composed a record of portents and anomalies.
entries.literal: Midway through his tenure as chancellor, he was dismissed and given the post of Palace Grandee; residing at his quarters, he composed a record of portentous anomalies.

entries.zh: 是時遼東高廟災，主父偃疾之，取其書奏之天子。
entries.en: Around that time, the High Ancestor's temple in Liaodong was struck by a disaster. Zhufu Yan, who bore a grudge against him, seized his writings and presented them to the emperor.
entries.literal: At that time, the High Ancestor's temple in Liaodong was damaged by a disaster. Zhufu Yan, who bore him a grudge, took his writings and presented them to the emperor.

entries.zh: 天子召諸生示其書，有刺譏。
entries.en: The emperor summoned the court scholars and showed them the writings, which contained pointed criticisms of the government.
entries.literal: The emperor summoned the scholars and showed them the writings, which contained pointed criticisms.

entries.zh: 董仲舒弟子呂步舒不知其師書，以為下愚。
entries.en: Dong Zhongshu's own disciple, Lu Bushu, failed to recognize his teacher's work and judged it to be the product of an inferior and foolish mind.
entries.literal: Dong Zhongshu's disciple Lu Bushu did not recognize his own teacher's work and judged it to be the product of an inferior and foolish mind.

entries.zh: 於是下董仲舒吏，當死，詔赦之。
entries.en: Dong Zhongshu was turned over to the judicial officials and sentenced to death, but an imperial pardon saved his life.
entries.literal: Thereupon Dong Zhongshu was handed over to the judicial officials and sentenced to death, but an imperial edict pardoned him.

entries.zh: 於是董仲舒竟不敢復言災異。
entries.en: From that day on, Dong Zhongshu never again dared to speak of portents and anomalies.
entries.literal: From then on, Dong Zhongshu ultimately never dared to speak of portentous anomalies again.

entries.zh: 蘭陵王臧既受詩，以事孝景帝為太子少傅，免去。
entries.en: Wang Zang of Lanling, having studied the Odes under Master Shen, served Emperor Jing as Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent, but was later dismissed from the post.
entries.literal: Wang Zang of Lanling, having received instruction in the Odes, served Emperor Jing as Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent, but was dismissed and departed.

entries.zh: 今上初即位，臧乃上書宿衛上，累遷，一歲中為郎中令。
entries.en: When the present emperor first ascended the throne, Wang Zang submitted a memorial and was assigned to the palace guard. Through successive promotions, he rose within a single year to become the Commandant of the Gentlemen of the Interior.
entries.literal: When the present emperor first ascended the throne, Zang submitted a memorial and was assigned to the palace guard; through successive promotions, within a single year he became the Commandant of the Gentlemen of the Interior.

entries.zh: 及代趙綰亦嘗受詩申公，綰為御史大夫。
entries.en: Zhao Wan of Dai had also studied the Odes under Master Shen. He rose to become the Imperial Secretary.
entries.literal: Zhao Wan of Dai had also once studied the Odes under Master Shen; Wan became the Imperial Secretary.

entries.zh: 綰、臧請天子，欲立明堂以朝諸侯，不能就其事，乃言師申公。
entries.en: Zhao Wan and Wang Zang petitioned the emperor to build a Hall of Light for receiving the feudal lords in audience. Unable to bring the project to fruition on their own, they recommended their teacher, Master Shen.
entries.literal: Wan and Zang petitioned the emperor, wishing to establish a Hall of Light for receiving audiences with the feudal lords; unable to bring the project to fruition, they then recommended their teacher, Master Shen.

entries.zh: 於是天子使使束帛加璧安車駟馬迎申公，弟子二人乘軺傳從。
entries.en: The emperor sent an envoy bearing bundles of silk and jade discs, together with a comfortable carriage drawn by four horses, to welcome Master Shen. Two of his disciples rode in a light carriage to accompany him.
entries.literal: Thereupon the emperor sent an envoy with bundles of silk and jade discs, along with a comfortable carriage drawn by four horses, to welcome Master Shen; two of his disciples rode in a light carriage and accompanied him.

entries.zh: 至，見天子。
entries.en: Upon his arrival, he was granted an audience with the emperor.
entries.literal: When he arrived, he had an audience with the emperor.

entries.zh: 天子問治亂之事，申公時已八十餘，老，對曰：「為治者不在多言，顧力行何如耳。」
entries.en: The emperor asked him about the principles of order and disorder. Master Shen, by then over eighty and frail with age, replied: "Good governance does not lie in many words — it lies only in the vigor of one's actions."
entries.literal: The emperor asked him about the principles of order and disorder. Master Shen was by then over eighty years old and aged; he replied: "Governing does not lie in many words, but only in how vigorously one acts."

entries.zh: 是時天子方好文詞，見申公對，默然。
entries.en: At that time the emperor was particularly enamored of eloquent rhetoric. Hearing Master Shen's blunt reply, he fell silent.
entries.literal: At that time, the emperor was particularly fond of fine words and literary expression; upon hearing Master Shen's reply, he fell silent.

entries.zh: 然已招致，則以為太中大夫，舍魯邸，議明堂事。
entries.en: Nevertheless, having already summoned him, the emperor appointed him Grand Palace Grandee, lodged him at the Lu embassy, and charged him with deliberating on the Hall of Light project.
entries.literal: Nevertheless, having already summoned him, the emperor appointed him Grand Palace Grandee, lodged him at the Lu embassy, and had him deliberate on the Hall of Light project.

entries.zh: 太皇竇太后好老子言，不說儒術，得趙綰、王臧之過以讓上，上因廢明堂事，盡下趙綰、王臧吏，後皆自殺。
entries.en: The Grand Empress Dowager Dou was devoted to the teachings of Laozi and had no use for Confucian learning. She seized upon the transgressions of Zhao Wan and Wang Zang to reproach the emperor. The emperor thereupon abandoned the Hall of Light project and turned Zhao Wan and Wang Zang over to the judicial officials. Both later took their own lives.
entries.literal: The Grand Empress Dowager Dou was fond of the teachings of Laozi and disliked Confucian learning. She found fault with Zhao Wan and Wang Zang and used their offenses to reproach the emperor. The emperor thereupon abandoned the Hall of Light project and handed Zhao Wan and Wang Zang over entirely to the judicial officials; both later took their own lives.

entries.zh: 申公亦疾免以歸，數年卒。
entries.en: Master Shen, too, was dismissed on account of illness and returned home. He died a few years later.
entries.literal: Master Shen was also dismissed on account of illness and returned home; he died several years later.

entries.zh: 清河王太傅轅固生者，齊人也。
entries.en: Yuan Gusheng, who served as Grand Tutor to the King of Qinghe, was a native of Qi.
entries.literal: Yuan Gusheng, Grand Tutor to the King of Qinghe, was a man of Qi.

entries.zh: 以治詩，孝景時為博士。
entries.en: Through his mastery of the Odes, he was appointed an erudite during the reign of Emperor Jing.
entries.literal: Through his mastery of the Odes, he became an erudite during the reign of Emperor Jing.

entries.zh: 與黃生爭論景帝前。
entries.en: He once engaged in a debate with Master Huang in the presence of Emperor Jing.
entries.literal: He engaged in a debate with Master Huang before Emperor Jing.

entries.zh: 黃生曰：「湯武非受命，乃弒也。」
entries.en: Master Huang declared: "Tang and Wu did not receive the Mandate of Heaven — what they did was regicide."
entries.literal: Master Huang said: "Tang and Wu did not receive the Mandate of Heaven; what they did was regicide."

entries.zh: 轅固生曰：「不然。
entries.en: Yuan Gusheng replied: "That is not so.
entries.literal: Yuan Gusheng said: "That is not so.

entries.zh: 夫桀紂虐亂，天下之心皆歸湯武，湯武與天下之心而誅桀紂，桀紂之民不為之使而歸湯武，湯武不得已而立，非受命為何？」
entries.en: Jie and Zhou were cruel and tyrannical, and the hearts of all under Heaven turned to Tang and Wu. Tang and Wu, acting in accord with the will of the people, punished Jie and Zhou. The people under Jie and Zhou refused to serve their rulers and turned to Tang and Wu instead. Tang and Wu had no choice but to take the throne. If this is not receiving the Mandate of Heaven, then what is?"
entries.literal: Jie and Zhou were cruel and tyrannical, and the hearts of all under Heaven turned to Tang and Wu. Tang and Wu, in accord with the hearts of all under Heaven, punished Jie and Zhou. The people of Jie and Zhou refused to serve them and turned to Tang and Wu. Tang and Wu had no choice but to establish themselves as rulers. If this is not receiving the Mandate, then what is?"

entries.zh: 黃生曰：「冠雖敝，必加於首；
entries.en: Master Huang replied: "A cap, however worn, must still be placed upon the head;
entries.literal: Master Huang said: "A cap, though worn out, must still be placed upon the head;

entries.zh: 履雖新，必關於足。
entries.en: shoes, however new, must still be worn on the feet.
entries.literal: shoes, though new, must still be placed upon the feet.

entries.zh: 何者，上下之分也。
entries.en: Why? Because this is the distinction between what is above and what is below.
entries.literal: Why? Because this is the distinction between high and low.

entries.zh: 今桀紂雖失道，然君上也；
entries.en: Jie and Zhou, though they lost the Way, were still the sovereign above;
entries.literal: Now Jie and Zhou, though they lost the Way, were still the rulers above;

entries.zh: 湯武雖聖，臣下也。
entries.en: Tang and Wu, though sages, were still subjects in rank.
entries.literal: Tang and Wu, though sages, were still subjects below.

entries.zh: 夫主有失行，臣下不能正言匡過以尊天子，反因過而誅之，代立踐南面，非弒而何也？」
entries.en: When the sovereign errs in conduct, if his subjects cannot speak forthrightly to correct his faults and thereby honor the Son of Heaven, but instead exploit those faults to execute him, take his place, and assume the throne — if that is not regicide, what is?"
entries.literal: When the ruler has erred in conduct, if his subjects cannot speak forthrightly to correct his faults and thereby uphold the Son of Heaven, but instead seize upon his faults to execute him, take his place, and face south as ruler — if this is not regicide, then what is?"

entries.zh: 轅固生曰：「必若所云，是高帝代秦即天子之位，非邪？」
entries.en: Yuan Gusheng retorted: "If what you say must hold, then was the High Emperor wrong to replace Qin and take the throne?"
entries.literal: Yuan Gusheng said: "If it must be as you say, then was the High Emperor wrong to replace Qin and assume the position of Son of Heaven?"

entries.zh: 於是景帝曰：「食肉不食馬肝，不為不知味；
entries.en: At this, Emperor Jing intervened: "A man who eats meat but refuses horse liver is not thereby ignorant of flavor;
entries.literal: At this, Emperor Jing said: "One who eats meat but does not eat horse liver is not considered ignorant of flavors;

entries.zh: 言學者無言湯武受命，不為愚。」
entries.en: a scholar who declines to speak of Tang and Wu receiving the Mandate is not thereby a fool."
entries.literal: a scholar who does not speak of Tang and Wu receiving the Mandate is not thereby foolish."

entries.zh: 遂罷。
entries.en: The debate was brought to a close.
entries.literal: The debate was thereupon ended.

entries.zh: 是後學者莫敢明受命放殺者。
entries.en: From then on, no scholar dared openly discuss the Mandate of Heaven or the deposing and slaying of rulers.
entries.literal: From this time on, no scholar dared openly discuss the subject of receiving the Mandate and deposing and killing rulers.

entries.zh: 竇太后好老子書，召轅固生問老子書。
entries.en: Empress Dowager Dou was fond of the writings of Laozi and summoned Yuan Gusheng to discuss them.
entries.literal: Empress Dowager Dou was fond of the book of Laozi and summoned Yuan Gusheng to discuss it.

entries.zh: 固曰：「此是家人言耳。」
entries.en: Yuan Gu replied: "This is merely the talk of a commoner."
entries.literal: Yuan Gu said: "This is merely the talk of a commoner."

entries.zh: 太后怒曰：「安得司空城旦書乎？」
entries.en: The Empress Dowager was enraged and said: "How is this any better than the penal laborers' texts?"
entries.literal: The Empress Dowager was furious and said: "How is this any better than the writings of convicts sentenced to hard labor?"

entries.zh: 乃使固入圈刺豕。
entries.en: She ordered Yuan Gu to enter the boar pen and fight a wild pig.
entries.literal: She then ordered Yuan Gu to enter the boar pen and fight a wild boar.

entries.zh: 景帝知太后怒而固直言無罪，乃假固利兵，下圈刺豕，正中其心，一刺，豕應手而倒。
entries.en: Emperor Jing, knowing the Empress Dowager was enraged but that Yuan Gu had spoken forthrightly and was blameless, secretly provided him with a sharp weapon. Yuan Gu descended into the pen, struck the boar straight through the heart, and with a single thrust the beast dropped dead.
entries.literal: Emperor Jing, knowing the Empress Dowager was angry but that Yuan Gu had spoken forthrightly and committed no crime, provided Yuan Gu with a sharp weapon. He went down into the pen to fight the boar, struck it straight through the heart, and with a single thrust the boar fell at his hand.

entries.zh: 太后默然，無以復罪，罷之。
entries.en: The Empress Dowager fell silent, having no further grounds to punish him, and let the matter drop.
entries.literal: The Empress Dowager was silent, having no further grounds to punish him, and dismissed the matter.

entries.zh: 居頃之，景帝以固為廉直，拜為清河王太傅。
entries.en: Before long, Emperor Jing, recognizing Yuan Gu as a man of integrity and forthright character, appointed him Grand Tutor to the King of Qinghe.
entries.literal: Before long, Emperor Jing, regarding Yuan Gu as a man of integrity and honesty, appointed him Grand Tutor to the King of Qinghe.

entries.zh: 久之，病免。
entries.en: In time, he was relieved of his duties on account of illness.
entries.literal: After a long time, he was dismissed on account of illness.

entries.zh: 韓生者，燕人也。
entries.en: Master Han was a native of Yan.
entries.literal: Master Han was a man of Yan.

entries.zh: 孝文帝時為博士，景帝時為常山王太傅。
entries.en: He served as an erudite under Emperor Wen and as Grand Tutor to the King of Changshan under Emperor Jing.
entries.literal: During the reign of Emperor Wen he served as an erudite, and during the reign of Emperor Jing he served as Grand Tutor to the King of Changshan.

entries.zh: 韓生推詩之意而為內外傳數萬言，其語頗與齊魯閒殊，然其歸一也。
entries.en: Master Han elaborated on the meaning of the Odes and composed Inner and Outer Commentaries amounting to tens of thousands of words. His language differed considerably from the traditions of Qi and Lu, yet the essential purport was the same.
entries.literal: Master Han developed the meaning of the Odes and composed Inner and Outer Commentaries amounting to tens of thousands of words; his language differed considerably from the traditions between Qi and Lu, yet their essential purport was one and the same.

entries.zh: 淮南賁生受之。
entries.en: Master Ben of Huainan received this transmission from him.
entries.literal: Master Ben of Huainan received the transmission from him.

entries.zh: 自是之後，而燕趙閒言詩者由韓生。
entries.en: From that time on, those who expounded the Odes in the lands between Yan and Zhao traced their tradition to Master Han.
entries.literal: From this time on, those who expounded the Odes in the region between Yan and Zhao traced their tradition to Master Han.

entries.zh: 韓生孫商為今上博士。
entries.en: Master Han's grandson, Shang, became an Erudite under the present emperor.
entries.literal: Master Han's grandson Shang became an erudite under the present emperor.

entries.zh: 胡毋生，齊人也。
entries.en: Humu Sheng was a native of Qi.
entries.literal: Humu Sheng was a man of Qi.

entries.zh: 孝景時為博士，以老歸教授。
entries.en: He served as an erudite during the reign of Emperor Jing and, upon reaching old age, returned home to teach.
entries.literal: During the reign of Emperor Jing, he served as an erudite; when old, he returned home to teach.

entries.zh: 齊之言春秋者多受胡毋生，公孫弘亦頗受焉。
entries.en: Most of the Spring and Autumn Annals scholars in Qi had studied under Humu Sheng, and Gongsun Hong himself received considerable instruction from him.
entries.literal: Many of those in Qi who expounded the Spring and Autumn Annals received their instruction from Humu Sheng, and Gongsun Hong also received considerable instruction from him.

entries.zh: 仲舒弟子遂者：蘭陵褚大，廣川殷忠，溫呂步舒。
entries.en: Among Dong Zhongshu's disciples who rose to success were Chu Da of Lanling, Yin Zhong of Guangchuan, and Lu Bushu of Wen.
entries.literal: Among Dong Zhongshu's disciples who achieved success were: Chu Da of Lanling, Yin Zhong of Guangchuan, and Lu Bushu of Wen.

entries.zh: 褚大至梁相。
entries.en: Chu Da rose to become Chancellor of Liang.
entries.literal: Chu Da rose to be Chancellor of Liang.

entries.zh: 步舒至長史，持節使決淮南獄，於諸侯擅專斷，不報，以春秋之義正之，天子皆以為是。
entries.en: Lu Bushu rose to the post of Chief Clerk. Bearing the imperial staff as an envoy, he adjudicated the case of the King of Huainan. Among the feudal lords he made independent judgments without awaiting approval, justifying his actions by the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals. The emperor approved of every decision he made.
entries.literal: Lu Bushu rose to Chief Clerk, and bearing the imperial staff as an envoy, adjudicated the case of the King of Huainan; among the feudal lords, he took it upon himself to make independent judgments without reporting back, justifying his actions by the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals. The emperor considered all his decisions correct.

entries.zh: 弟子通者，至於命大夫；
entries.en: Among his proficient disciples, some rose to the rank of appointed grandee;
entries.literal: Of his disciples who achieved proficiency, some rose to the rank of appointed grandee;

entries.zh: 為郎、謁者、掌故者以百數。
entries.en: while those who served as Gentlemen, Ushers, or Keepers of Precedents numbered in the hundreds.
entries.literal: those who served as Gentlemen, Ushers, or Keepers of Precedents numbered in the hundreds.

entries.zh: 而董仲舒子及孫皆以學至大官。
entries.en: Dong Zhongshu's sons and grandsons all attained high office through their scholarship.
entries.literal: Dong Zhongshu's sons and grandsons all attained high office through their learning.

entries.zh: 太史公曰：余讀功令，至於廣厲學官之路，未嘗不廢書而嘆也。
entries.en: The Grand Historian remarks: Whenever I read the imperial statutes and reach the provisions for expanding the pathways of official scholarship, I cannot help but put down my book and sigh.
entries.literal: The Grand Historian says: When I read the imperial statutes and came to the provisions for broadening and encouraging the paths of academic officials, I never failed to set aside my book and sigh.

entries.zh: 曰：嗟乎！
entries.en: The Grand Historian went on: Alas!
entries.literal: The Grand Historian continued: Alas!

entries.zh: 夫周室衰而關雎作，幽厲微而禮樂壞，諸侯恣行，政由彊國。
entries.en: As the Zhou dynasty waned, the ode "Guan Ju" was composed; as Kings You and Li grew feeble, ritual and music fell to ruin. The feudal lords acted as they pleased, and political power rested with the strongest states.
entries.literal: When the House of Zhou declined, the Guan Ju ode was composed; when Kings You and Li were diminished, ritual and music fell into ruin; the feudal lords acted willfully, and governance was dictated by the powerful states.

entries.zh: 故孔子閔王路廢而邪道興，於是論次詩書，修起禮樂。
entries.en: Confucius, grieving that the Way of the kings had fallen into disuse while heterodox doctrines flourished, set about editing the Odes and the Documents and reviving the rites and music.
entries.literal: Therefore, Confucius grieved that the royal way had been abandoned and heterodox paths had arisen, and so he edited and arranged the Odes and Documents, and restored ritual and music.

entries.zh: 適齊聞韶，三月不知肉味。
entries.en: When he traveled to Qi and heard the Shao music performed, for three months he was so enraptured that he did not notice the taste of meat.
entries.literal: When he visited Qi and heard the Shao music, for three months he did not notice the taste of meat.

entries.zh: 自衛返魯，然後樂正，雅頌各得其所。
entries.en: Only after his return from Wei to Lu did he set the music in order, restoring Ya and Song each to its proper place.
entries.literal: After he returned to Lu from Wei, the music was then corrected, and the Ya and Song sections each found their proper place.

entries.zh: 世以混濁莫能用，是以仲尼干七十餘君無所遇，曰「茍有用我者，期月而已矣」。
entries.en: The age was so mired in chaos that none would employ him. Confucius appealed to more than seventy rulers, yet none took him in. He said, "Were anyone to employ me, within a single year I would have something to show for it."
entries.literal: The age was so muddied and turbid that no one could employ him; thus Confucius solicited more than seventy rulers but found no acceptance, saying, "If anyone were to employ me, within a single year I could accomplish something."

entries.zh: 西狩獲麟，曰「吾道窮矣」。
entries.en: When a qilin was captured during a hunt in the west, he said, "My Way has come to its end."
entries.literal: When a unicorn was captured during a hunt in the west, he said, "My Way has reached its end."

entries.zh: 故因史記作春秋，以當王法，其辭微而指博，後世學者多錄焉。
entries.en: Drawing upon the historical records, he composed the Spring and Autumn Annals as a standard of kingly governance. Its language is subtle, yet its implications are vast, and scholars of later ages have widely studied and transmitted it.
entries.literal: Therefore, drawing on the historical records, he composed the Spring and Autumn Annals to serve as the law of a true king; its language is subtle yet its meaning far-reaching, and scholars of later generations have widely transmitted it.

entries.zh: 且緩急，人之所時有也。
entries.en: After all, desperate need is something that comes to every person sooner or later.
entries.literal: Moreover, the need for urgent help is something that comes to everyone from time to time.

entries.zh: 太史公曰：昔者虞舜窘於井廩，伊尹負於鼎俎，傅說匿於傅險，呂尚困於棘津，夷吾桎梏，百里飯牛，仲尼畏匡，菜色陳、蔡。
entries.en: The Grand Historian remarks: In the old days, Emperor Shun was nearly killed in a well and a granary. Yi Yin labored among the pots and cutting boards. Fu Yue hid himself at the cliffs of Fu. Lu Shang was reduced to desperate straits at Jijin. Guan Zhong wore fetters. Baili Xi fed cattle for a living. Confucius was besieged at Kuang and went hungry until his face turned sallow between Chen and Cai.
entries.literal: The Grand Historian said: In ancient times, Emperor Shun was trapped in a well and a granary; Yi Yin bore the burdens of the cooking vessels; Fu Yue hid at the cliff of Fu; Lu Shang was stranded at Jijin; Guan Zhong wore fetters; Baili Xi herded cattle; Confucius was threatened at Kuang, and his face grew gaunt at Chen and Cai.

entries.zh: 此皆學士所謂有道仁人也，猶然遭此菑，況以中材而涉亂世之末流乎？
entries.en: All of these were the very paragons that scholars call men of virtue and benevolence — yet even they suffered such calamities. How much worse, then, for ordinary people struggling through the dregs of a disordered age?
entries.literal: These were all what scholars call men of the Way and benevolence, yet they still suffered such calamities — how much more so for those of ordinary talent who wade through the turbid currents of a disordered age?

entries.zh: 其遇害何可勝道哉！
entries.en: The calamities such men suffer are beyond all telling!
entries.literal: The harm they encountered — how can it be fully described!

entries.zh: 鄙人有言曰：「何知仁義，已饗其利者為有德。」
entries.en: Common folk have a saying: "What does anyone know about benevolence and righteousness? Whoever reaps the profits is the one called virtuous."
entries.literal: The common people have a saying: "What do they know of benevolence and righteousness? Those who have enjoyed the benefits are considered virtuous."

entries.zh: 故伯夷丑周，餓死首陽山，而文武不以其故貶王；
entries.en: Bo Yi despised the Zhou conquest and starved himself to death on Mount Shouyang, yet Kings Wen and Wu were nonetheless regarded as kings on that account.
entries.literal: Thus, Bo Yi despised the Zhou dynasty and starved to death on Mount Shouyang, yet Kings Wen and Wu were not diminished in their kingship on his account;

entries.zh: 跖、蹻暴戾，其徒誦義無窮。
entries.en: Robber Zhi and Zhuang Qiao were violent and cruel, yet their followers sang praises to their righteousness without end.
entries.literal: Zhi and Qiao were cruel and violent, yet their followers praised their righteousness without end.

entries.zh: 由此觀之，「竊鉤者誅，竊國者侯，侯之門仁義存」，非虛言也。
entries.en: Seen in this light, the old saying is no empty proverb: "Steal a belt buckle, and you are executed; steal a kingdom, and you are made a lord; at the lord's gate, the virtues of benevolence and righteousness take up residence."
entries.literal: Looking at it from this perspective, "He who steals a belt buckle is executed, he who steals a kingdom becomes a feudal lord, and at the lord's gate benevolence and righteousness dwell" — these are not empty words.

entries.zh: 魯朱家者，與高祖同時。
entries.en: Zhu Jia of Lu lived in the same era as Emperor Gaozu.
entries.literal: Zhu Jia of Lu was a contemporary of Emperor Gaozu.

entries.zh: 魯人皆以儒教，而朱家用俠聞。
entries.en: The people of Lu were all devoted to Confucian learning, but Zhu Jia won his fame through knight-errantry.
entries.literal: The people of Lu all followed Confucian teachings, yet Zhu Jia was known for his chivalry.

entries.zh: 所藏活豪士以百數，其餘庸人不可勝言。
entries.en: The fugitives and heroes he sheltered and saved numbered in the hundreds; the ordinary folk he helped were too many to count.
entries.literal: The heroes he sheltered and saved numbered in the hundreds, and the ordinary people beyond that were too many to count.

entries.zh: 然終不伐其能，歆其德，諸所嘗施，唯恐見之。
entries.en: Yet he never boasted of his abilities or took pride in his virtuous deeds, and of all the people he had once helped, he dreaded nothing more than running into them again.
entries.literal: Yet he never boasted of his abilities or gloried in his virtue; as for those he had once helped, he feared nothing more than to encounter them again.

entries.zh: 振人不贍，先從貧賤始。
entries.en: When he gave aid to those in need, he always started with the poorest and most humble.
entries.literal: When he aided people in need, he always began with the poorest and most humble.

entries.zh: 家無餘財，衣不完采，食不重味，乘不過軥牛。
entries.en: His household had no spare wealth. His clothes bore no fine colors. His meals had no second course. His only conveyance was an ox-drawn cart.
entries.literal: His household had no surplus wealth, his clothes were not finely colored, his meals had no second dish, and his conveyance was no more than a yoked ox.

entries.zh: 專趨人之急，甚己之私。
entries.en: He devoted himself entirely to the urgent needs of others, putting them above his own private concerns.
entries.literal: He devoted himself wholly to the urgent needs of others, more than to his own private affairs.

entries.zh: 既陰脫季布將軍之阸，及布尊貴，終身不見也。
entries.en: After he had secretly rescued General Ji Bu from peril, once Ji Bu rose to a position of honor, Zhu Jia never sought him out again for the rest of his life.
entries.literal: After he had secretly rescued General Ji Bu from danger, once Ji Bu rose to honor and eminence, Zhu Jia never saw him again for the rest of his life.

entries.zh: 自關以東，莫不延頸願交焉。
entries.en: From the Pass eastward, there was no one who did not crane their neck, hoping for the chance to befriend him.
entries.literal: From the Pass eastward, there was no one who did not crane their necks and desire to form a friendship with him.

entries.zh: 是時濟南瞷氏、陳周庸亦以豪聞，景帝聞之，使使盡誅此屬。
entries.en: Around this time, the Jian clan of Jinan and Zhou Yong of Chen were also renowned as local strongmen. Emperor Jing heard of them and dispatched agents to have them all put to death.
entries.literal: At this time, the Jian clan of Jinan and Zhou Yong of Chen were also known as local strongmen; Emperor Jing heard of them and dispatched envoys to have them all executed.

entries.zh: 其後代諸白、梁韓無辟、陽翟薛兄、陜韓孺紛紛復出焉。
entries.en: After them, new figures emerged one after another: the Bai clan of Dai, Han Wubi of Liang, Xue Xiong of Yangzhai, and Han Ru of Shan.
entries.literal: Afterwards, the Bai of Dai, Han Wubi of Liang, Xue Xiong of Yangzhai, and Han Ru of Shan emerged one after another.

entries.zh: 及徙豪富茂陵也，解家貧，不中訾，吏恐，不敢不徙。
entries.en: When the government ordered the relocation of wealthy and powerful families to Maoling, Guo Jie's family was too poor to meet the property threshold, but the officials were afraid of him and did not dare leave him behind.
entries.literal: When the wealthy and powerful were relocated to Maoling, Guo Jie's family was poor and did not meet the property qualification, yet the officials were afraid and did not dare to leave him behind.

entries.zh: 衛將軍為言：「郭解家貧不中徙。」
entries.en: General Wei Qing spoke to the emperor on his behalf, saying: "The Guo Jie household is poor and does not qualify for relocation."
entries.literal: General Wei Qing spoke on his behalf, saying: "The Guo Jie household is poor and does not qualify for relocation."

entries.zh: 上曰：「布衣權至使將軍為言，此其家不貧。」
