entries.en: The emperor said: "A commoner whose influence is great enough to make a general speak on his behalf — his household is not poor."
entries.literal: The emperor said: "A commoner whose influence extends to making a general speak on his behalf — his household cannot be poor."

entries.zh: 解家遂徙。
entries.en: And so the Guo Jie household was relocated after all.
entries.literal: So the Guo Jie household was relocated after all.

entries.zh: 諸公送者出千餘萬。
entries.en: The farewell gifts from the worthies who saw him off totaled more than ten million cash.
entries.literal: The farewell gifts contributed by the various worthies who saw him off amounted to more than ten million cash.

entries.zh: 軹人楊季主子為縣掾，舉徙解。
entries.en: It was the son of Yang Jizhu, a fellow native of Zhi who served as a county clerk, who had nominated Guo Jie for the relocation.
entries.literal: The son of Yang Jizhu of Zhi served as a county clerk and had nominated Guo Jie for relocation.

entries.zh: 解兄子斷楊掾頭。
entries.en: Guo Jie's nephew cut off the head of the young clerk Yang.
entries.literal: Guo Jie's brother's son cut off the head of Clerk Yang.

entries.zh: 由此楊氏與郭氏為仇。
entries.en: From this point on, the Yang and Guo clans became bitter enemies.
entries.literal: From this the Yang clan and the Guo clan became enemies.

entries.zh: 解入關，關中賢豪知與不知，聞其聲，爭交驩解。
entries.en: When Guo Jie arrived in the Guanzhong region, the local worthies and strongmen — whether they knew him personally or not — had all heard his name and competed to befriend him.
entries.literal: When Guo Jie entered the Pass, the worthies and strongmen of the Guanzhong region, whether they knew him or not, having heard his reputation, competed to befriend him.

entries.zh: 解為人短小，不飲酒，出未嘗有騎。
entries.en: Guo Jie was short in stature and did not drink. When he went out, he never rode with a mounted escort.
entries.literal: Guo Jie was short and small in stature, did not drink wine, and when he went out he never had a mounted escort.

entries.zh: 已又殺楊季主。
entries.en: Before long, someone also killed Yang Jizhu himself.
entries.literal: Then someone killed Yang Jizhu as well.

entries.zh: 楊季主家上書，人又殺之闕下。
entries.en: The Yang family submitted a memorial to the throne, but the person who delivered it was murdered right at the palace gates.
entries.literal: The Yang Jizhu family submitted a memorial to the throne, but the person who delivered it was killed at the gates of the palace.

entries.zh: 上聞，乃下吏捕解。
entries.en: When the emperor heard of this, he ordered the authorities to arrest Guo Jie.
entries.literal: When the emperor heard of this, he ordered officials to arrest Guo Jie.

entries.zh: 解亡，置其母家室夏陽，身至臨晉。
entries.en: Guo Jie fled, settling his mother and household at Xiayang while he himself made for Linjin.
entries.literal: Guo Jie fled, placing his mother and household at Xiayang, while he himself went to Linjin.

entries.zh: 臨晉籍少公素不知解，解冒，因求出關。
entries.en: Ji Shaogong of Linjin had never met Guo Jie. Guo Jie approached him under a false name and through him arranged to slip past the border checkpoint.
entries.literal: Ji Shaogong of Linjin did not previously know Guo Jie; Guo Jie came to him under an assumed identity and through him sought to pass through the barrier.

entries.zh: 籍少公已出解，解轉入太原，所過輒告主人家。
entries.en: After Ji Shaogong had helped him through the checkpoint, Guo Jie traveled on into Taiyuan, revealing his identity to his hosts at each stop along the way.
entries.literal: After Ji Shaogong had helped Guo Jie pass through, Guo Jie made his way into Taiyuan, and at each stop he would reveal his identity to his host household.

entries.zh: 吏逐之，跡至籍少公。
entries.en: The authorities pursued him and traced his trail back to Ji Shaogong.
entries.literal: The officials pursued him and traced his trail to Ji Shaogong.

entries.zh: 少公自殺，口絕。
entries.en: Ji Shaogong killed himself, sealing the secret with his death.
entries.literal: Shaogong killed himself, and his mouth was silenced forever.

entries.zh: 久之，乃得解。
entries.en: After a long search, Guo Jie was finally captured.
entries.literal: After a long time, Guo Jie was finally captured.

entries.zh: 窮治所犯，為解所殺，皆在赦前。
entries.en: When the authorities exhaustively investigated his crimes, they found that all the killings attributed to Guo Jie had occurred before the most recent amnesty.
entries.literal: When all his offenses were exhaustively investigated, the killings attributed to Guo Jie had all occurred before the amnesty.

entries.zh: 軹有儒生侍使者坐，客譽郭解，生曰：「郭解專以姦犯公法，何謂賢！」
entries.en: In Zhi, a Confucian scholar was seated in the company of the imperial envoy. When a guest began praising Guo Jie, the scholar spoke up: "Guo Jie does nothing but use wickedness to break the law — what is worthy about that!"
entries.literal: In Zhi, there was a Confucian scholar sitting in attendance on the imperial envoy; a guest was praising Guo Jie, and the scholar said: "Guo Jie does nothing but use wickedness to violate the public law — what is worthy about that!"

entries.zh: 解客聞，殺此生，斷其舌。
entries.en: When Guo Jie's followers heard what the scholar had said, they killed him and cut out his tongue.
entries.literal: When Guo Jie's followers heard of this, they killed the scholar and cut out his tongue.

entries.zh: 吏以此責解，解實不知殺者。
entries.en: The authorities charged Guo Jie with the crime, but in truth he did not know who had done the killing.
entries.literal: The officials blamed Guo Jie for this, but in truth Guo Jie did not know who the killer was.

entries.zh: 殺者亦竟絕，莫知為誰。
entries.en: The killer vanished completely, and no one ever discovered who it was.
entries.literal: The killer also vanished without a trace, and no one ever learned who it was.

entries.zh: 吏奏解無罪。
entries.en: The officials submitted their finding that Guo Jie was not guilty.
entries.literal: The officials reported that Guo Jie was not guilty.

entries.zh: 御史大夫公孫弘議曰：「解布衣為任俠行權，以睚眥殺人，解雖弗知，此罪甚於解殺之。
entries.en: The Imperial Counselor Gongsun Hong argued: "Guo Jie is a commoner who practices knight-errantry and wields unauthorized power. Men are killed over the slightest grudge on his account. Even if he did not know of it, this crime is greater than if he had killed them with his own hand.
entries.literal: The Imperial Counselor Gongsun Hong argued: "Guo Jie, a commoner, practices knight-errantry and exercises unauthorized power; men are killed over the merest grudge on his account. Even though Guo Jie may not have known, this crime is worse than if Guo Jie had killed them himself.

entries.zh: 當大逆無道。」
entries.en: He should be condemned for the crime of high treason."
entries.literal: He should be charged with the crime of great treason and depravity."

entries.zh: 遂族郭解翁伯。
entries.en: And so the entire clan of Guo Jie was exterminated.
entries.literal: And so the entire clan of Guo Jie, styled Wengbo, was exterminated.

entries.zh: 韓子曰：「儒以文亂法，而俠以武犯禁。」
entries.en: Han Feizi once wrote: "Confucian scholars subvert the law with their writings, and wandering knights defy authority with their swords."
entries.literal: Han Feizi said: "The Confucians use their writings to undermine the law, while the knights-errant use their martial prowess to violate the prohibitions."

entries.zh: 二者皆譏，而學士多稱於世云。
entries.en: Both were censured, yet scholars have always found admirers in the world.
entries.literal: Both of these are criticized, yet scholars are much praised by the world.

entries.zh: 至如以術取宰相卿大夫，輔翼其世主，功名俱著於春秋，固無可言者。
entries.en: Those who rose to become chancellors and ministers through political craft, who served as their lord's right hand, whose deeds and reputations fill the histories — they need no further comment.
entries.literal: As for those who by craft attained the positions of chancellor, ministers, and grandees, who assisted and supported their rulers, their achievements and fame all recorded in the annals, there is nothing that needs to be said about them.

entries.zh: 及若季次、原憲，閭巷人也，讀書懷獨行君子之德，義不茍合當世，當世亦笑之。
entries.en: Then there were men like Ji Ci and Yuan Xian — common folk of the lanes and alleys who cherished their books and upheld the solitary virtues of the true gentleman. They refused on principle to bend to the age, and the age laughed at them in return.
entries.literal: As for Ji Ci and Yuan Xian, they were men of the back alleys, who read books and held fast to the virtues of the solitary-minded gentleman, whose integrity refused to compromise with their times, and their times also laughed at them.

entries.zh: 故季次、原憲終身空室蓬戶，褐衣疏食不厭。
entries.en: So Ji Ci and Yuan Xian lived out their days in bare rooms behind wattle doors, clad in rough cloth and eating thin gruel, yet never once complained.
entries.literal: Thus, Ji Ci and Yuan Xian lived their whole lives in empty rooms with bramble-woven doors, in coarse garments and meager food without complaint.

entries.zh: 死而已四百餘年，而弟子志之不倦。
entries.en: More than four hundred years after their deaths, their disciples still honor their memory without flagging.
entries.literal: They have been dead for over four hundred years, yet their disciples record them without tiring.

entries.zh: 今游俠，其行雖不軌於正義，然其言必信，其行必果，已諾必誠，不愛其軀，赴士之阸困，既已存亡死生矣，而不矜其能，羞伐其德，蓋亦有足多者焉。
entries.en: Now consider the wandering knights. Their conduct may not conform to orthodox morality, yet when they give their word they keep it, when they commit to action they see it through, and when they make a promise they honor it with their lives. They throw themselves into the perils of others without sparing their own bodies, having stared down life and death without flinching — and yet they never boast of their abilities or trumpet their virtue. Surely there is much in them to admire.
entries.literal: Now the wandering knights, though their conduct may not conform to standards of righteousness, yet their words are always trustworthy, their actions always decisive, their promises always kept; they do not spare their own bodies, they rush to the aid of gentlemen in distress, having already risked life and death, yet they do not boast of their abilities, are ashamed to brag of their virtues — there is indeed much in them worthy of praise.

entries.zh: 昔以色幸者多矣。
entries.en: In times past, many rose to favor on the strength of their beauty.
entries.literal: In the past, those who were favored through their appearance were many.

entries.zh: 至漢興，高祖至暴抗也，然籍孺以佞幸；
entries.en: When the Han dynasty was founded, Emperor Gaozu was as fierce and unyielding a man as ever lived, yet even he kept Ji Ru as a favorite through flattery and charm.
entries.literal: When the Han dynasty arose, Gaozu was most violent and domineering, yet Ji Ru gained favor through flattery and charm;

entries.zh: 孝惠時有閎孺。
entries.en: During the reign of Emperor Hui, there was Hong Ru.
entries.literal: In the time of Emperor Xiaohui, there was Hong Ru.

entries.zh: 此兩人非有材能，徒以婉佞貴幸，與上臥起，公卿皆因關說。
entries.en: Neither of these two men possessed any talent whatsoever. They rose to honor and favor solely through their ingratiating ways, sharing the emperor's bed, and every minister and noble at court sought to press their petitions through them.
entries.literal: These two men had no talent or ability; they were honored and favored solely through their suppliant flattery, sharing the emperor's bed and board, and all the ministers and nobles sought to intercede through them.

entries.zh: 故孝惠時郎侍中皆冠鵕鸃，貝帶，傅脂粉，化閎、籍之屬也。
entries.en: And so during Emperor Hui's reign, every palace gentleman and attendant at court wore caps adorned with junyi feathers and belts studded with cowrie shells, their faces powdered and rouged—all in imitation of Hong Ru and Ji Ru.
entries.literal: Thus, during Emperor Xiaohui's reign, all the palace gentlemen and attendants wore caps adorned with junyi bird feathers, belts decorated with cowrie shells, and applied rouge and powder, imitating the fashion of Hong Ru, Ji Ru, and their kind.

entries.zh: 兩人徙家安陵。
entries.en: Both men moved their households to Anling.
entries.literal: The two men relocated their families to Anling.

entries.zh: 孝文時中寵臣，士人則鄧通，宦者則趙同、北宮伯子。
entries.en: Among the favored intimates at Emperor Wen's court, the gentleman was Deng Tong, and the eunuchs were Zhao Tong and Beigong Bozi.
entries.literal: Among the inner court favorites during Emperor Xiaowen's reign, among gentlemen there was Deng Tong, and among eunuchs there were Zhao Tong and Beigong Bozi.

entries.zh: 北宮伯子以愛人長者；
entries.en: Beigong Bozi won favor because he cared for others and bore himself as a dignified elder.
entries.literal: Beigong Bozi was favored because he cared for others and was a man of dignified elderliness;

entries.zh: 而趙同以星氣幸，常為文帝參乘；
entries.en: Zhao Tong found favor through his knowledge of astrology and divination by cloud formations, and he regularly rode beside Emperor Wen in the imperial chariot.
entries.literal: Zhao Tong was favored through his knowledge of astrology and the study of vapors, and he regularly served as Emperor Wen's chariot companion;

entries.zh: 鄧通無伎能。
entries.en: Deng Tong possessed no particular skill or talent.
entries.literal: Deng Tong had no skills or abilities.

entries.zh: 鄧通，蜀郡南安人也，以濯船為黃頭郎。
entries.en: Deng Tong hailed from Nan'an in the Commandery of Shu. He had entered palace service as a Yellow-Cap Boatman, poling vessels along the imperial waterways.
entries.literal: Deng Tong was a man of Nan'an in the Commandery of Shu, who served as a Yellow-Cap Boatman by rowing boats.

entries.zh: 孝文帝夢欲上天，不能，有一黃頭郎從後推之上天，顧見其衣裻帶后穿。
entries.en: Emperor Wen once dreamed that he was striving to ascend to heaven but could not reach it, when a Yellow-Cap Boatman came up behind him and pushed him aloft. Glancing back, the emperor noticed that the man's robe was torn at the seam in the back.
entries.literal: Emperor Xiaowen dreamed that he wanted to ascend to heaven but could not, when a Yellow-Cap Boatman pushed him from behind up to heaven. Looking back, he saw that the man's robe had a hole in the seam at the back.

entries.zh: 覺而之漸臺，以夢中陰目求推者郎，即見鄧通，其衣后穿，夢中所見也。
entries.en: When he woke, the emperor made his way to the Jian Terrace and quietly scanned the attendants, searching for the man from his dream. His gaze fell at once on Deng Tong, whose robe was torn at the back—exactly as he had seen it in the dream.
entries.literal: After waking, he went to the Jiantai terrace, and secretly searched with his eyes among the attendants for the man who had pushed him in the dream. He immediately spotted Deng Tong, whose robe was torn in the back—just as he had seen in the dream.

entries.zh: 召問其名姓，姓鄧氏，名通，文帝說焉，尊幸之日異。
entries.en: The emperor summoned the man and asked his name. His surname was Deng, his given name Tong. Emperor Wen was delighted, and from that day forward his favor toward Deng Tong only grew.
entries.literal: He summoned the man and asked his name and surname. His surname was Deng, his given name Tong. Emperor Wen was pleased, and honored and favored him more with each passing day.

entries.zh: 通亦願謹，不好外交，雖賜洗沐，不欲出。
entries.en: For his part, Tong was circumspect and cautious, with no taste for outside socializing. Even on his leave days for bathing, he preferred not to go out.
entries.literal: Tong was also careful and prudent, not fond of socializing outside. Even when granted leave days for bathing, he did not wish to go out.

entries.zh: 於是文帝賞賜通巨萬以十數，官至上大夫。
entries.en: Emperor Wen showered him with gifts totaling tens of millions of cash, and raised his rank to Senior Grand Master.
entries.literal: Thereupon Emperor Wen bestowed rewards on Tong amounting to tens of millions, and his official rank reached Senior Grand Master.

entries.zh: 文帝時時如鄧通家遊戲。
entries.en: From time to time, Emperor Wen would visit Deng Tong's residence to amuse himself.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen would from time to time go to Deng Tong's home to amuse himself.

entries.zh: 然鄧通無他能，不能有所薦士，獨自謹其身以媚上而已。
entries.en: Yet Deng Tong had no other talent and never recommended a single person for office. He simply took care to conduct himself properly and please the emperor—nothing more.
entries.literal: Yet Deng Tong had no other ability and could not recommend any scholars for office; he merely conducted himself carefully to please the emperor, and nothing more.

entries.zh: 上使善相者相通，曰「當貧餓死」。
entries.en: The emperor summoned a skilled physiognomist to read Tong's face. The verdict was grim: "This man is fated to die in poverty, of starvation."
entries.literal: The emperor had a skilled physiognomist examine Tong's face, who said, 'He is destined to die of poverty and starvation.'

entries.zh: 文帝曰：「能富通者在我也。
entries.en: Emperor Wen said, "The power to make Tong rich rests with me.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen said, 'The power to make Tong rich lies with me.

entries.zh: 何謂貧乎？」
entries.en: How could he ever become poor?"
entries.literal: How can one speak of poverty?'

entries.zh: 於是賜鄧通蜀嚴道銅山，得自鑄錢，「鄧氏錢」布天下。
entries.en: Thereupon he granted Deng Tong the copper mines at Yandao in Shu, with the right to mint his own coins. The "Deng coins" soon circulated throughout the empire.
entries.literal: Thereupon he granted Deng Tong the copper mountains at Yandao in Shu, with permission to mint his own coins. 'Deng clan coins' spread throughout the empire.

entries.zh: 其富如此。
entries.en: Such was the measure of his wealth.
entries.literal: Such was the extent of his wealth.

entries.zh: 文帝嘗病癰，鄧通常為帝唶吮之。
entries.en: Once Emperor Wen developed an abscess, and Deng Tong would regularly suck the pus from it for him.
entries.literal: Emperor Wen once suffered from an abscess, and Deng Tong would regularly suck the pus from it for the emperor.

entries.zh: 文帝不樂，從容問通曰：「天下誰最愛我者乎？」
entries.en: Emperor Wen, ill at ease, asked Tong casually, "Who in all the realm loves me the most?"
entries.literal: Emperor Wen, feeling unhappy, casually asked Tong, 'Who in all the realm loves me the most?'

entries.zh: 通曰：「宜莫如太子。」
entries.en: Tong replied, "Surely none more than the Crown Prince."
entries.literal: Tong said, 'Surely none more so than the Crown Prince.'

entries.zh: 太子入問病，文帝使唶癰，唶癰而色難之。
entries.en: When the Crown Prince came to inquire about the emperor's illness, Emperor Wen bade him suck the abscess. The prince did so, but his face betrayed his disgust.
entries.literal: When the Crown Prince came in to inquire about the emperor's illness, Emperor Wen had him suck the abscess. He sucked the abscess, but his expression showed his difficulty and reluctance.

entries.zh: 已而聞鄧通常為帝唶吮之，心慚，由此怨通矣。
entries.en: Later, when the Crown Prince learned that Deng Tong had been doing this all along without complaint, he was filled with shame, and from that day bore a bitter grudge against Tong.
entries.literal: Afterward, when he heard that Deng Tong regularly sucked the abscess for the emperor, he felt ashamed in his heart, and from this point on bore a grudge against Tong.

entries.zh: 及文帝崩，景帝立，鄧通免，家居。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen died and Emperor Jing took the throne, Deng Tong was removed from office and lived at home.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen passed away and Emperor Jing was enthroned, Deng Tong was dismissed from office and remained at home.

entries.zh: 居無何，人有告鄧通盜出徼外鑄錢。
entries.en: Before long, someone accused Deng Tong of illegal minting beyond the frontier passes.
entries.literal: Before long, someone reported that Deng Tong had been illicitly casting coins beyond the frontier passes.

entries.zh: 下吏驗問，頗有之，遂竟案，盡沒入鄧通家，尚負責數巨萬。
entries.en: The matter was handed to the officials for investigation. Substantial evidence was found, and the case was prosecuted to its end. The entire Deng household was stripped of its property, yet Tong still owed debts amounting to tens of millions of cash.
entries.literal: The case was referred to officials for investigation, and considerable evidence was found. The case was pursued to its conclusion, and all of Deng Tong's household property was confiscated, yet he still owed debts of tens of millions.

entries.zh: 長公主賜鄧通，吏輒隨沒入之，一簪不得著身。
entries.en: Whenever the Elder Princess sent gifts to Deng Tong, officials would swoop in at once to confiscate them. He was not allowed to keep so much as a hairpin.
entries.literal: The Elder Princess gave gifts to Deng Tong, but officials would immediately follow and confiscate them, so that not a single hairpin was allowed to remain on his person.

entries.zh: 於是長公主乃令假衣食。
entries.en: In the end, the Elder Princess could only arrange to lend him clothes and food.
entries.literal: Thereupon the Elder Princess arranged to lend him clothing and food.

entries.zh: 竟不得名一錢，寄死人家。
entries.en: He ended his days without a single coin to his name, dying as a dependent in someone else's household.
entries.literal: In the end he could not call a single coin his own, and died as a dependent in another person's household.

entries.zh: 今天子中寵臣，士人則韓王孫嫣，宦者則李延年。
entries.en: Among the current emperor's favored intimates, the gentleman is Han Yan, a scion of the former Kings of Han, and the eunuch is Li Yannian.
entries.literal: Among the current emperor's inner court favorites, among gentlemen there is Han Yan, grandson of the King of Han, and among eunuchs there is Li Yannian.

entries.zh: 嫣者，弓高侯孽孫也。
entries.en: Han Yan was a collateral grandson of the Marquis of Gonggao.
entries.literal: Yan was a collateral grandson of the Marquis of Gonggao.

entries.zh: 今上為膠東王時，嫣與上學書相愛。
entries.en: When the current emperor was still the King of Jiaodong, Yan studied writing with him, and the two grew deeply attached.
entries.literal: When the current emperor was King of Jiaodong, Yan studied writing with the emperor and the two became close.

entries.zh: 及上為太子，愈益親嫣。
entries.en: When the emperor became Crown Prince, his intimacy with Yan only deepened.
entries.literal: When the emperor became Crown Prince, he became ever more intimate with Yan.

entries.zh: 嫣善騎射，善佞。
entries.en: Yan excelled at riding and archery, and was adept at the art of flattery.
entries.literal: Yan was skilled at riding and archery, and skilled at flattery.

entries.zh: 上即位，欲事伐匈奴，而嫣先習胡兵，以故益尊貴，官至上大夫，賞賜擬於鄧通。
entries.en: When the emperor took the throne and resolved to wage war against the Xiongnu, Yan's prior training in the military arts of the steppe peoples made him all the more valued. His rank rose to Senior Grand Master, and the gifts he received rivaled those once lavished on Deng Tong.
entries.literal: When the emperor ascended the throne, he wished to undertake campaigns against the Xiongnu, and Yan had already practiced the arts of barbarian warfare. For this reason his rank and honor increased further, his official rank reached Senior Grand Master, and the rewards bestowed on him were comparable to those of Deng Tong.

entries.zh: 時嫣常與上臥起。
entries.en: In those days, Yan shared the emperor's bed and table.
entries.literal: At that time, Yan regularly shared the emperor's bed and board.

entries.zh: 江都王入朝，有詔得從入獵上林中。
entries.en: The King of Jiangdu came to court on an audience visit and was granted an imperial edict allowing him to join the emperor's hunt in the Shanglin Park.
entries.literal: The King of Jiangdu came to court, and received an edict permitting him to accompany the emperor on a hunt in the Shanglin Park.

entries.zh: 天子車駕蹕道未行，而先使嫣乘副車，從數十百騎，騖馳視獸。
entries.en: Before the emperor's own chariot had even set out along the cleared road, he sent Yan ahead in a secondary imperial carriage, attended by scores of mounted riders, galloping through the park to scout the game.
entries.literal: Before the emperor's chariot and procession had set out along the cleared road, he first sent Yan ahead riding in a secondary imperial chariot, attended by scores of mounted horsemen, galloping to scout the game.

entries.zh: 江都王望見，以為天子，辟從者，伏謁道傍。
entries.en: The King of Jiangdu saw this procession from a distance and, mistaking it for the emperor's own, waved his retinue aside and prostrated himself in greeting by the roadside.
entries.literal: The King of Jiangdu, seeing this from afar, took it for the emperor. He dismissed his attendants and prostrated himself in greeting by the roadside.

entries.zh: 嫣驅不見。
entries.en: Yan swept past without so much as a glance.
entries.literal: Yan drove past without acknowledging him.

entries.zh: 既過，江都王怒，為皇太后泣曰：「請得歸國入宿衛，比韓嫣。」
entries.en: After the procession had passed, the King of Jiangdu was livid. He went weeping before the Empress Dowager and said, "I beg leave to surrender my kingdom and join the Palace Guard, if only to be treated as well as Han Yan."
entries.literal: After the party had passed, the King of Jiangdu was furious. He wept before the Empress Dowager and said, 'I beg permission to return my kingdom and enter the Palace Guard, so as to be treated like Han Yan.'

entries.zh: 太后由此嗛嫣。
entries.en: From that moment, the Empress Dowager harbored a deep resentment toward Yan.
entries.literal: The Empress Dowager from this point bore a grudge against Yan.

entries.zh: 嫣侍上，出入永巷不禁，以姦聞皇太后。
entries.en: In his attendance upon the emperor, Yan came and went freely through the Yongxiang, the palace women's quarters, without restriction. Word of his illicit affairs reached the Empress Dowager.
entries.literal: Yan, in his attendance upon the emperor, came and went through the Yongxiang palace women's quarters without restriction. Reports of his illicit liaisons reached the Empress Dowager.

entries.zh: 皇太后怒，使使賜嫣死。
entries.en: The Empress Dowager was furious and dispatched a messenger to order Yan to take his own life.
entries.literal: The Empress Dowager was furious and sent a messenger to bestow death upon Yan.

entries.zh: 上為謝，終不能得，嫣遂死。
entries.en: The emperor pleaded for clemency, but the Empress Dowager would not relent, and Yan was put to death.
entries.literal: The emperor pleaded on Yan's behalf, but in the end could not obtain a pardon. Yan thereupon died.

entries.zh: 而案道侯韓說，其弟也，亦佞幸。
entries.en: Han Yue, the Marquis of Andao, was Yan's younger brother, and he too became a court favorite.
entries.literal: The Marquis of Andao, Han Yue, was Yan's younger brother, and he too gained favor through flattery.

entries.zh: 孝景帝時，中無寵臣，然獨郎中令周文仁，仁寵最過庸，乃不甚篤。
entries.en: During Emperor Jing's reign, there were no notable court favorites. Only Zhou Ren, the Palace Gentleman Commander, enjoyed favor somewhat beyond the ordinary, and even that was not very deep.
entries.literal: During Emperor Jing's reign, there were no inner court favorites. Only the Palace Gentleman Commander Zhou Ren enjoyed favor beyond the ordinary, but even that favor was not very deep.

entries.zh: 李延年，中山人也。
entries.en: Li Yannian hailed from the kingdom of Zhongshan.
entries.literal: Li Yannian was a man from Zhongshan.

entries.zh: 父母及身兄弟及女，皆故倡也。
entries.en: His parents, he himself, his brothers, and his sisters had all been entertainers.
entries.literal: His parents, he himself, his brothers, and his sisters had all formerly been entertainers.

entries.zh: 延年坐法腐，給事狗中。
entries.en: Yannian was convicted of a crime and sentenced to castration, after which he was set to work in the palace dog kennels.
entries.literal: Yannian was convicted of a crime and punished with castration, and was assigned to serve in the dog kennels.

entries.zh: 而平陽公主言延年女弟善舞，上見，心說之，及入永巷，而召貴延年。
entries.en: Princess Pingyang mentioned that Yannian's younger sister was a gifted dancer. When the emperor saw her perform, he was captivated. After she was taken into the palace, the emperor summoned Yannian and raised him to a position of honor.
entries.literal: Princess Pingyang mentioned that Yannian's younger sister was skilled at dancing. The emperor saw her and was pleased. After she entered the Yongxiang palace quarters, the emperor summoned and elevated Yannian.

entries.zh: 延年善歌，為變新聲，而上方興天地祠，欲造樂詩歌弦之。
entries.en: Yannian was a gifted singer and composer of new melodies. At that time the emperor was instituting grand sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, and wished to commission poems and hymns to be set to music for the ceremonies.
entries.literal: Yannian was skilled at singing and at composing new melodies. The emperor was at that time promoting sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, and wished to create musical poems and songs to be set to stringed instruments.

entries.zh: 延年善承意，弦次初詩。
entries.en: Yannian had a gift for anticipating the emperor's wishes, and deftly set the newly composed poems to music.
entries.literal: Yannian was skilled at anticipating the emperor's wishes, and set the newly composed poems to music in sequence.

entries.zh: 其女弟亦幸，有子男。
entries.en: His younger sister likewise became an imperial favorite and bore the emperor a son.
entries.literal: His younger sister was also favored by the emperor, and bore a son.

entries.zh: 延年佩二千石印，號協聲律。
entries.en: Yannian was granted the seal of a two-thousand-bushel official and bore the title Harmonizer of Tones and Pitches.
entries.literal: Yannian wore the seal of a two-thousand-bushel official, and held the title of Harmonizer of Tones and Pitches.

entries.zh: 與上臥起，甚貴幸，埒如韓嫣也。
entries.en: He shared the emperor's bed and table, honored and favored to a degree that rivaled Han Yan himself.
entries.literal: He shared the emperor's bed and board, and was greatly honored and favored, on a par with Han Yan.

entries.zh: 久之，寖與中人亂，出入驕恣。
entries.en: In time, he began carrying on illicit affairs with the palace women and grew ever more brazen and unrestrained.
entries.literal: As time passed, he gradually became involved in licentious affairs with palace women, and grew arrogant and unrestrained in his comings and goings.

entries.zh: 及其女弟李夫人卒后，愛弛，則禽誅延年昆弟也。
entries.en: After his sister, Lady Li, died, the emperor's affection cooled, and Yannian and his brothers were arrested and put to death.
entries.literal: After his younger sister, Lady Li, died, the emperor's affection waned, and Yannian and his brothers were arrested and executed.
